items.stem: A technologist prepares 10% formalin by mixing 10 mL of commercial formalin (37–40% formaldehyde) with 90 mL of water. What is the approximate formaldehyde concentration of the working solution?
items.why: Commercial formalin is a saturated solution containing roughly 37–40% formaldehyde gas. Diluting it 1 in 10 gives "10% formalin," which actually contains **about 4% formaldehyde**. The "10%" refers to the dilution of stock formalin, not to the formaldehyde content.

whyNot.0: Ten percent is the dilution of the stock formalin, not the formaldehyde concentration.
whyNot.2: Roughly 37–40% is the formaldehyde content of the undiluted commercial stock, before the 1:10 dilution.
whyNot.3: A 1% formaldehyde solution would be far weaker than routine 10% formalin and would fix tissue poorly.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Sections of a congested spleen fixed in unbuffered 10% formalin show fine brown-black, birefringent granules lying outside cells. Which practice would best have prevented this artifact?
options: Adding glacial acetic acid to the formalin
Washing the tissue in running water for 24 hours after fixation
Buffering the formalin to a neutral pH
Post-fixing the tissue in Zenker's fluid
items.why: The granules are formalin pigment (acid formaldehyde hematin), which forms when acidic formalin reacts with hemoglobin in blood-rich tissue. It forms when formalin turns acidic, so **buffering formalin to neutral pH (neutral buffered formalin)** prevents it. Once formed, it can be removed with alcoholic picric acid.

whyNot.0: Acidifying formalin favors acid hematin formation and would make the pigment worse.
whyNot.1: Washing in water does not dissolve formalin pigment and does nothing to stop it forming during fixation.
whyNot.3: Zenker's fluid contains mercuric chloride and would add mercury pigment rather than prevent formalin pigment.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation artifacts and pigments); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Tissue fixed in Zenker's fluid shows black-brown granular deposits scattered across the section. Before staining, the deposits should be removed by treating the sections with:
items.why: Zenker's fluid contains mercuric chloride, which leaves a mercury pigment in tissue. It is removed by **iodine (e.g., Lugol's or alcoholic iodine), which converts it to mercuric iodide, followed by sodium thiosulfate**, which removes the brown iodine stain left behind.

whyNot.0: Alcoholic picric acid is used to remove formalin (acid formaldehyde hematin) pigment, not mercury pigment.
whyNot.2: Acid alcohol is a differentiator for regressive hematoxylin staining; it does not dissolve mercury deposits.
whyNot.3: Dilute ammonia water is a bluing agent after hematoxylin and does not remove mercury pigment.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Mercuric fixatives and pigment removal); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A femoral head is being decalcified in a nitric acid solution. Which method of checking whether decalcification is complete is considered the most accurate?
options: Bending or probing the specimen with a needle
Weighing the specimen to see if it has lost weight
Visual inspection for loss of opacity
items.why: Calcium deposits are radio-opaque, so an X-ray shows even small foci of remaining calcium. **Radiography is regarded as the most accurate end-point test**; the chemical (calcium oxalate) test on the used fluid is a practical alternative for acid decalcifiers.

whyNot.0: Probing or bending is the least reliable method and can damage the tissue and introduce artifacts.
whyNot.2: Weight change is less sensitive than radiography and does not show where residual calcium remains.
whyNot.3: Visual inspection cannot detect small residual calcium deposits inside the specimen.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Decalcification: end-point determination); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: During processing, a block of tissue turns milky and opaque when transferred from the last alcohol into xylene. What is the most likely cause?
options: The tissue was left too long in xylene
The tissue was over-fixed in formalin
Dehydration was incomplete, so water remained in the tissue
The paraffin bath was too hot
items.why: Xylene does not mix with water, so any water left in the tissue makes it look cloudy. **Milkiness on entering the clearing agent means dehydration was incomplete**. The tissue should go back through fresh absolute alcohol before clearing again.

whyNot.0: Prolonged exposure to xylene makes tissue hard and brittle; it does not make it milky.
whyNot.1: Over-fixation affects staining and antigenicity but does not cause turbidity in xylene.
whyNot.3: The paraffin bath comes after clearing, so its temperature cannot explain a change seen when the tissue enters xylene.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: dehydration and clearing); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A large brain specimen has been embedded in celloidin. Which microtome is traditionally used to cut it, with the knife set obliquely and both block and knife kept wet with 70% alcohol?
items.why: Celloidin blocks must stay moist and are cut slowly with a long oblique stroke. **The sliding microtome** is designed for this, with the knife set at an angle and the block and blade kept wet with 70% alcohol.

whyNot.0: The rotary microtome is the standard instrument for serial paraffin sections, not for wet celloidin blocks.
whyNot.2: The rocking microtome is a simple instrument for small paraffin blocks and is unsuitable for large celloidin blocks.
whyNot.3: The ultramicrotome cuts ultrathin resin sections for electron microscopy.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy; celloidin technique); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: In a regressive H&E method using Harris hematoxylin, sections are deliberately overstained. Which step then selectively removes excess hematoxylin until only the nuclei stay stained?
options: Bluing in Scott's tap water substitute
items.why: In regressive staining, tissue is overstained and the excess dye is then removed in a controlled way. **Differentiation in acid alcohol (dilute HCl in 70% alcohol)** strips hematoxylin from the cytoplasm and background while the nuclei stay stained. Bluing follows to turn the remaining hematoxylin blue and insoluble.

whyNot.0: Bluing raises the pH to change hematoxylin from red to blue; it does not remove excess dye.
whyNot.2: Eosin adds pink cytoplasmic staining and does not remove hematoxylin.
whyNot.3: Xylene clears the dehydrated section for mounting and plays no part in differentiation.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Hematoxylin and eosin); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A pathologist suspects fatty change in a liver biopsy and requests an Oil Red O stain. Which type of section should be prepared?
options: A routine paraffin section from NBF-fixed tissue
A paraffin section from Carnoy-fixed tissue
items.why: Routine processing through alcohols and clearing agents dissolves most neutral lipids, so they are lost before staining. **Lipid stains such as Oil Red O need frozen sections**, which skip dehydration and clearing (the tissue may be fixed in formalin first).

whyNot.0: Paraffin processing uses alcohols and xylene, which extract the lipids the stain is meant to show.
whyNot.2: Carnoy's fluid itself contains alcohol and chloroform, which dissolve lipids, and paraffin processing removes more.
whyNot.3: Celloidin embedding also uses alcohol and ether, which dissolve lipids.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Lipid staining); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: In a well-stained Papanicolaou smear, the cytoplasm of intermediate and parabasal squamous cells is blue-green. Which dye is chiefly responsible for this color?
items.why: The EA polychrome counterstain contains eosin Y and light green SF yellowish. **Light green stains the cytoplasm of metabolically active, less mature cells (intermediate and parabasal) blue-green**, while eosin stains mature superficial cells pink.

whyNot.0: Orange G (in OG-6) stains keratinized cytoplasm orange, not the cytoplasm of intermediate cells.
whyNot.1: Eosin Y gives the pink cytoplasm of mature superficial squamous cells.
whyNot.3: Bismarck brown is a traditional EA component that contributes little to the final staining and does not make cytoplasm blue-green.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Cytology: Papanicolaou stain)

items.stem: A cervical smear for Papanicolaou staining has just been spread on a slide. What is the recommended routine fixation?
options: Immediate immersion in 95% ethyl alcohol while the smear is still wet
items.why: Pap smears are wet-fixed: they go into the fixative before any drying occurs. **95% ethyl alcohol** is the standard fixative, and placing the smear in it immediately prevents air-drying artifact, which ruins nuclear detail.

whyNot.1: Air-drying followed by methanol is the approach for Romanowsky-type stains, not the Pap stain.
whyNot.2: Formalin is a tissue fixative and is not used routinely for Pap smears.
whyNot.3: Bouin's solution is a picric-acid tissue fixative and is not the standard for cervical smears.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Cytology: fixation of smears)

items.stem: A patient dies several days after a cerebral infarct. Which pattern of necrosis is expected in the infarcted brain tissue?
items.why: Brain tissue has abundant lytic enzymes and little supporting connective tissue, so dead tissue is digested into a soft, fluid-filled area. For this reason **ischemic necrosis of the central nervous system is liquefactive**, unlike infarcts in most solid organs.

whyNot.0: Coagulative necrosis is typical of hypoxic death in solid organs such as the heart and kidney, not the brain.
whyNot.2: Caseous necrosis is the cheese-like necrosis typical of tuberculous granulomas.
whyNot.3: Fat necrosis is typical of injury to fatty tissue, such as in acute pancreatitis.

items.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (Cell injury and cell death)

items.stem: During an autopsy examination, the gradual drop in body temperature after death until it matches the surrounding temperature is called:
items.why: **Algor mortis is post-mortem cooling of the body** toward room temperature, and is one of the signs used to estimate the time since death.

whyNot.0: Rigor mortis is the stiffening of muscles after death.
whyNot.1: Livor mortis (hypostasis) is the purplish discoloration in dependent parts as blood settles.
whyNot.3: Autolysis is the breakdown of cells by their own enzymes, not a change in temperature.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Autopsy); forensic pathology texts

items.stem: A Ziehl–Neelsen stain is requested on a lung biopsy. The technologist stains a section known to contain acid-fast bacilli on the same run as the patient slide. What is the main purpose of this section?
options: To estimate the number of organisms in the patient's tissue
To confirm that the reagents and procedure worked correctly in that run
To serve as a negative control for nonspecific staining
To check whether the patient's tissue was adequately fixed
items.why: A known-positive control tissue goes through the same reagents and steps as the patient slide. **If the control stains as expected, the run is valid**, and a negative patient result can be trusted rather than blamed on a faulty reagent or step.

whyNot.0: The control holds no information about how many organisms are in the patient's tissue.
whyNot.2: A section known to contain the target is a positive control, not a negative control.
whyNot.3: Fixation of the patient's tissue is judged from the patient's own section, not from a separate control block.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Quality control in histopathology)

items.stem: A laboratory manager reviews monthly turnaround times, compares them with the target set in the quality manual, and introduces corrective action where the target was missed. Which management function is this?
items.why: **Controlling** means measuring actual performance, comparing it with set standards, and correcting the gaps. Reviewing turnaround times against a target and acting on misses is a direct example.

whyNot.0: Planning sets objectives and decides in advance how to reach them; it does not measure results already achieved.
whyNot.1: Organizing arranges people, tasks and resources into a working structure.
whyNot.2: Directing (leading) is guiding, motivating and supervising staff while the work is being done.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Management functions)

items.stem: In a study comparing two staining protocols, the investigator concludes there is a significant difference (p < 0.05), but in reality the protocols perform equally. What kind of error has been made?
options: Measurement error due to poor precision
items.why: **A type I error is rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true**, which here means declaring a difference that does not exist. Its probability is the significance level (alpha) chosen by the investigator.

whyNot.1: A type II error is the opposite: failing to reject a false null hypothesis, which misses a real difference.
whyNot.2: Sampling bias is a systematic flaw in how subjects are selected, not the statistical error of rejecting a true null hypothesis.
whyNot.3: Poor precision adds random variation to measurements, but the scenario describes a wrong decision about the null hypothesis.

items.ref: Standard biostatistics references (e.g., Daniel, Biostatistics: A Foundation for Analysis in the Health Sciences)

items.stem: Researchers select 100 women with confirmed cervical carcinoma and 200 women without it, then review their records for past HPV infection. Which study design is this?
items.why: Subjects are chosen by whether they already have the disease, and the investigators then look back for past exposure. **Selecting on outcome and comparing prior exposures is the defining feature of a case-control study**.

whyNot.0: A cohort study selects people by exposure status and follows them forward to see who develops the disease.
whyNot.2: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and disease at a single point in time without selecting on outcome.
whyNot.3: A randomized controlled trial assigns an intervention by chance and follows outcomes; no intervention is assigned here.

items.ref: Gordis Epidemiology (Study designs)

items.stem: Under Section 19 of RA 5527 (Philippine Medical Technology Act of 1969), what are the minimum general average and the lowest permissible rating in any major subject for passing the board examination?
options: General average of at least 75%, with no major subject below 50%
General average of at least 75%, with no major subject below 60%
General average of at least 70%, with no major subject below 50%
General average of at least 80%, with no major subject below 75%
items.why: Section 19 requires **a general average of at least seventy-five per cent with no rating below fifty per cent in any of the major subjects**. It also adds that the candidate must not have failed in at least sixty per cent of the subjects, computed by their relative weights.

whyNot.1: The 60% figure in Section 19 refers to the proportion of subjects failed (by relative weight), not to a minimum rating per subject.
whyNot.2: Seventy per cent appears elsewhere in the law as amended (registration as medical laboratory technician), not as the passing general average.
whyNot.3: Neither 80% nor 75% per subject is a requirement in Section 19.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 19

items.stem: Under Section 21 of RA 5527 as amended by PD 498, a person who failed the medical technology board examination may still be registered as a medical laboratory technician if the general rating obtained was at least:
items.why: As amended by PD 498 (1974), Section 21 allows registration as a medical laboratory technician of a person who **failed the board examination but obtained a general rating of at least 70%**. PD 498 also defines a medical laboratory technician as one qualified to assist a medical technologist and/or qualified pathologist.

whyNot.0: Sixty per cent is not the threshold in Section 21; 60% appears in Section 19 in connection with subjects failed.
whyNot.1: Sixty-five per cent is not stated anywhere in the amended Section 21.
whyNot.3: Seventy-two per cent is not the statutory figure; the law sets the floor at 70%.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 21, as amended by PD 498 (1974)

items.stem: After notice and hearing, the Board finds that a registered medical technologist should be suspended rather than have the certificate revoked. Under Section 24 of RA 5527, what is the maximum period of suspension?
items.why: Section 24 allows the Board to reprimand, suspend, or revoke a certificate of registration after due notice and hearing. **Suspension may not exceed two years**, and revocation requires a unanimous vote of the Board.

whyNot.0: Six months is not the limit; it is the minimum prison term in the penal provisions of Section 29.
whyNot.1: One year is shorter than the limit the statute actually sets.
whyNot.3: Five years exceeds the statutory maximum for suspension.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 24

items.stem: Under the Newborn Screening Act of 2004 (RA 9288), when should newborn screening be performed?
options: Within the first 12 hours of life
After 24 hours of life but not later than 3 days from complete delivery
At any time before the infant turns 30 days old
items.why: Section 6 of RA 9288 states that newborn screening **shall be performed after twenty-four (24) hours of life but not later than three (3) days from complete delivery**. Section 4 separately defines a newborn as a child from complete delivery to 30 days old.

whyNot.0: Sampling within 12 hours is earlier than the law allows and can give false-negative results for some disorders.
whyNot.2: Seven to 14 days is well beyond the 3-day limit set by Section 6.
whyNot.3: Thirty days is the age limit in the definition of "newborn" in Section 4, not the screening window.

items.ref: RA 9288 Sec. 6 (definition in Sec. 4)

items.stem: A 16-year-old comes to a testing facility on her own and asks for a voluntary HIV test. Under RA 11166 (Philippine HIV and AIDS Policy Act), whose consent is required?
options: The adolescent herself, with no need for parental consent
The attending physician on her behalf
items.why: Section 29 of RA 11166 provides that for a person **fifteen (15) to below eighteen (18) years of age, consent to voluntary HIV testing is obtained from the child without the need of consent from a parent or guardian**. Parental or guardian consent is the rule for those below 15 or who are mentally incapacitated, with exceptions such as pregnancy or high-risk behavior.

whyNot.0: Parental or guardian consent applies mainly to persons below 15 or who are mentally incapacitated, not to a 16-year-old.
whyNot.2: A social worker is not named as the consenting party for a 16-year-old requesting a voluntary test.
whyNot.3: A physician cannot consent on a patient's behalf to voluntary testing; the law requires the person's own informed consent.

items.stem: Under Section 36 of the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165), how long is a drug test certificate from an accredited drug testing center valid?
options: Three months from the date of issue
Six months from the date of issue
One year from the date of issue
Two years from the date of issue
items.why: Section 36 provides that drug test certificates issued by accredited drug testing centers **shall be valid for a one-year period from the date of issue**. The same section requires a positive screening test to be confirmed by a confirmatory test such as gas chromatography/mass spectrometry.

whyNot.0: Three months is not the validity period stated in Section 36.
whyNot.1: Six months is shorter than the one-year validity the law gives.
whyNot.3: Two years is longer than the validity the law allows.

items.ref: RA 9165 Sec. 36

items.stem: Under the National Blood Services Act of 1994 (RA 7719), commercial blood banks were to be phased out over what initial period after the Act took effect?
options: One year, with no extension allowed
Two years, extendable by the Secretary of Health for up to two more years
Three years, extendable by the Secretary of Health for one more year
items.why: Section 7 of RA 7719 directs that **all commercial blood banks shall be phased out over a period of two (2) years after the Act takes effect, extendable to a maximum of two (2) years by the Secretary**. This reflects the Act's policy that blood is a service, not a commodity, and should come from voluntary, non-remunerated donors.

whyNot.0: The law sets a two-year period and explicitly allows an extension.
whyNot.2: Neither the five-year period nor an extension by Congress is in Section 7.
whyNot.3: The phase-out period is two years, not three, and the extension can be up to two years.

items.ref: RA 7719 Sec. 7

items.stem: A man dies in a hospital without having made a legacy of his organs and with no known objection on record. Under the Organ Donation Act of 1991 (RA 7170), who is first in the order of priority to donate his body or organs?
options: His son or daughter of legal age
His brother or sister of legal age
items.why: Section 4 of RA 7170 lists who may donate a decedent's body or organs, in order: **the spouse first**, then a son or daughter of legal age, either parent, a brother or sister of legal age, and the guardian. This order applies when there is no actual notice of contrary intentions by the decedent or of opposition by a member of the immediate family.

whyNot.0: A son or daughter of legal age comes second, after the spouse.
whyNot.1: Either parent comes third in the order of priority.
whyNot.3: A brother or sister of legal age comes fourth.

items.ref: RA 7170 Sec. 4

items.stem: Under the Continuing Professional Development Act of 2016 (RA 10912), CPD is made a mandatory requirement for:
options: Renewal of the Professional Identification Card (PIC)
Initial issuance of the certificate of registration
items.why: Section 10 of RA 10912 makes **CPD a mandatory requirement for renewal of the Professional Identification Card** of all registered and licensed professionals. It applies after licensure, not as a condition to take the examination.

whyNot.0: Eligibility for the board examination is set by each profession's law (for MT, RA 5527 Sec. 16), not by CPD units.
whyNot.2: Oath-taking follows passing the examination and does not depend on CPD.
whyNot.3: The initial certificate of registration is issued upon passing the examination, before any CPD is required.

items.stem: A mentally competent adult outpatient, after the phlebotomy procedure has been fully explained, refuses venipuncture. The medical technologist does not draw blood, documents the refusal, and informs the requesting physician. Which bioethical principle is mainly being respected?
items.why: **Autonomy** is a competent person's right to make informed decisions about his or her own body, including refusing a procedure. Respecting an informed refusal, and reporting it rather than overriding it, upholds this principle.

whyNot.0: Beneficence is the duty to act for the patient's good; on its own it could be misused to justify overriding the refusal.
whyNot.1: Non-maleficence is the duty to avoid harm; it is not the main issue in honoring an informed refusal.
whyNot.2: Justice concerns fair distribution of care and resources among patients.

items.ref: Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics

items.stem: In describing a disease, pathologists separate its cause from the sequence of cellular and molecular events that follow the initial injury and lead to the disease. That sequence of events is called the:
items.why: Etiology is the cause of a disease, while **pathogenesis is the mechanism, the chain of events from the initial stimulus to the expression of disease**. Both are core aspects of a disease process, along with the morphologic changes and clinical manifestations.

whyNot.0: Etiology refers to the cause or origin of the disease (e.g., a virus or a gene mutation), not the sequence of events that follows.
whyNot.2: Prognosis is the predicted outcome or course of a disease, not its mechanism of development.
whyNot.3: Morphology refers to the structural (gross and microscopic) changes in cells and tissues, which are the result of pathogenesis rather than the sequence itself.

items.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (Introduction to pathology)

items.stem: A patient develops a moon face, central obesity, and thin skin after months of high-dose prednisone therapy for an autoimmune disease. A condition caused by medical treatment in this way is described as:
items.why: The disorder here was produced by the drug the physician prescribed. **A disease or condition caused by a medical treatment, procedure, or practitioner is called iatrogenic**.

whyNot.0: Idiopathic means the cause is unknown, whereas here the cause (glucocorticoid therapy) is clearly identified.
whyNot.1: Nosocomial refers to an infection acquired in a hospital or health-care facility; this condition is a drug effect, not an infection.
whyNot.3: Congenital means present at birth; this condition appeared in adulthood after treatment.

items.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary

items.stem: Years after an episode of acute rheumatic fever, a patient is found to have scarred, narrowed mitral valve leaflets. The valve damage, a lasting condition that results from the earlier disease, is best termed a:
items.why: **A sequela is a lasting abnormal condition that follows and results from a previous disease or injury**. Chronic rheumatic heart disease with mitral stenosis is a classic sequela of acute rheumatic fever.

whyNot.0: A prodrome is the set of early, nonspecific symptoms that appear before the full disease develops, not a late consequence.
whyNot.1: Remission is a lessening or disappearance of the signs and symptoms of a disease, not a permanent after-effect.
whyNot.2: An exacerbation is a worsening of an existing disease, whereas the valve scarring is a lasting result of a past one.

items.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (The heart: rheumatic heart disease)

items.stem: Which fixing agent preserves tissue mainly by forming methylene bridges that cross-link proteins, and is therefore classed as an additive, non-coagulant fixative?
items.why: **Formaldehyde reacts with protein side chains and forms methylene bridges between them**, cross-linking proteins into a gel without coagulating them. It adds itself to the tissue, so it is an additive, non-coagulant fixative.

whyNot.0: Ethanol fixes by dehydrating and coagulating (denaturing) proteins; it does not add to the tissue or form cross-links.
whyNot.2: Acetone is a coagulant, dehydrating fixative used mainly for cold fixation of frozen sections and enzymes, not a cross-linker.
whyNot.3: Acetic acid precipitates nucleoproteins and swells tissue; it is used in mixtures to counteract shrinkage, not as a protein cross-linker.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: mechanisms of formaldehyde); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A liver biopsy is submitted for demonstration of glycogen storage. Which of the following fixatives, an alcohol-based mixture, is best suited to preserve the glycogen?
items.why: Glycogen is water-soluble and can leach out of tissue in aqueous fixatives. **Carnoy's fluid (absolute ethanol, chloroform, and glacial acetic acid) is a non-aqueous alcoholic fixative that preserves glycogen well**, along with nucleic acids.

whyNot.0: Zenker's fluid is an aqueous mercuric chloride–dichromate–acetic acid fixative; it is valued for nuclear and connective tissue detail, not glycogen.
whyNot.1: Flemming's fluid contains osmium tetroxide and chromic acid and is used mainly for nuclear structures and for fat, not glycogen.
whyNot.3: Helly's fluid is an aqueous mercuric chloride–dichromate fixative favored for hematopoietic tissue and cytoplasmic granules, not glycogen.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: alcoholic fixatives, Carnoy's fluid); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A renal biopsy is divided, and one small piece is sent for transmission electron microscopy. Which fixative is routinely used for the primary fixation of this piece?
items.why: **Buffered glutaraldehyde (typically about 2.5–4%) is the standard primary fixative for electron microscopy**, because its two aldehyde groups cross-link proteins rapidly and preserve fine structure. The tissue is then usually post-fixed in osmium tetroxide.

whyNot.1: Osmium tetroxide is used mainly as the secondary (post-) fixative, which fixes lipids and adds electron density, after the glutaraldehyde step.
whyNot.2: Formalin can be used when nothing better is available, but its slower, reversible cross-linking gives poorer ultrastructure than glutaraldehyde.
whyNot.3: Bouin's fluid contains picric and acetic acids, which damage membranes and ultrastructure, so it is not used for electron microscopy.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Electron microscopy: fixation)

items.stem: A breast core biopsy will be tested for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2. According to the ASCO/CAP guideline recommendations, how long should it be fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin?
options: Exactly 24 hours, no more and no less
items.why: ASCO/CAP recommends that breast specimens for ER, PR, and HER2 testing be fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin for **6 to 72 hours**, with the time to fixation (cold ischemia time) kept within 1 hour. Under-fixation and over-fixation can both give false-negative results.

whyNot.0: One to four hours is under-fixation; formalin has not adequately cross-linked the tissue, which can lead to false-negative receptor results.
whyNot.2: Fixing for 96 hours or longer is over-fixation; excessive cross-linking masks epitopes and can reduce staining.
whyNot.3: The guideline gives an acceptable range rather than a single fixed time, so a strict 24-hour requirement is not correct.

items.ref: ASCO/CAP Guideline Recommendations for HER2 Testing in Breast Cancer and for ER/PR Testing (pre-analytic requirements); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Immunohistochemistry: fixation)

items.stem: In routine paraffin processing, what is the main purpose of the clearing step that follows dehydration?
options: To replace alcohol with a paraffin-miscible solvent
To remove the remaining water from the tissue
To harden the tissue before it is embedded
To make the tissue transparent for gross inspection
items.why: Paraffin does not mix with alcohol, so the alcohol must be replaced by a reagent that is miscible with both alcohol and paraffin. **Clearing (dealcoholization) replaces the dehydrant with a solvent such as xylene that paraffin can then displace**. The transparency that results is only a side effect that gave the step its name.

whyNot.1: Water is removed during dehydration, which comes before clearing; clearing agents such as xylene do not mix with water.
whyNot.2: Hardening is mainly the role of fixation and of the paraffin itself; clearing is not meant to harden tissue, and over-exposure can make it brittle.
whyNot.3: Tissue does become translucent, which is where the name comes from, but that is incidental and not the purpose of the step.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: clearing); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A paraffin oven's thermostat fails, and tissues are infiltrated in paraffin held at about 70 °C, well above the wax's melting point of 56–58 °C. What effect on the tissue is most likely?
options: Incomplete removal of the clearing agent from the tissue
Softening that makes the tissue mushy on cutting
No effect, since higher heat only speeds infiltration
items.why: Paraffin should be kept only a few degrees above its melting point. **Overheating causes excessive shrinkage and makes the tissue hard and brittle**, so sections crumble or crack on the microtome.

whyNot.1: Higher temperature, if anything, speeds the evaporation and displacement of the clearing agent; leftover clearant results from too few or too short wax changes.
whyNot.2: Mushy, soft tissue suggests incomplete fixation, dehydration, or infiltration, not overheating.
whyNot.3: Excess heat does not just speed infiltration; it damages the tissue, which is why ovens are kept close to the wax melting point.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: infiltration with paraffin wax); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A skin punch biopsy is being embedded in paraffin. How should it be oriented so that the section shows the epidermis, dermis, and subcutis together?
options: Flat, epidermis facing the bottom of the mold
Flat, epidermis facing the top of the mold
Anywhere in the mold, as long as it is centered
On edge, with the cut perpendicular to the surface
items.why: The pathologist needs to see every layer of the skin in one section. **Embedding the specimen on edge places the plane of section perpendicular to the epidermal surface**, so each section runs from epidermis through dermis into subcutis.

whyNot.0: Lying the biopsy flat with the surface down makes the first sections cut parallel to the surface, showing only the epidermis rather than all layers.
whyNot.1: With the surface up, the sections are still parallel to the skin surface; the first cuts pass through the subcutis or dermis only.
whyNot.2: Orientation is not optional for skin; random placement gives tangential sections that can make the layers impossible to interpret.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Embedding: orientation of specimens); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: While cutting a paraffin ribbon on a rotary microtome, the technologist notices a vertical score line running through every section at the same position. What is the most likely cause?
options: A nick in the cutting edge of the knife
The paraffin is too soft for the room temperature
The knife tilt is too great, causing chatter
items.why: A defect that repeats at the same spot in every section must come from something fixed in the path of the block. **A nick or damaged area on the knife edge scores a line into each section**; the fix is to move to another part of the blade or replace it.

whyNot.1: Paraffin that is too soft causes compressed, crumpled sections that stick together, not a sharp line at a fixed position.
whyNot.2: Chatter from too great a tilt or a loose knife produces horizontal ridges or thick-and-thin bands across the section, not a vertical line.
whyNot.3: Incomplete dehydration leaves the tissue soft and crumbly so that it falls out of the wax, rather than producing a consistent scratch line.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: section faults and remedies); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Which microtome is the one most commonly used to cut routine paraffin sections in a hospital histopathology laboratory?
items.why: **The rotary (Minot) microtome is the standard instrument for routine paraffin sections**. Turning its wheel moves the block up and down past a fixed knife, producing serial ribbons at a set thickness.

whyNot.0: The sliding microtome is mainly used for celloidin-embedded and very large or hard blocks, not routine paraffin work.
whyNot.1: The freezing microtome is for cutting frozen tissue and has largely been replaced by the cryostat; it is not used for paraffin blocks.
whyNot.3: The ultramicrotome cuts ultrathin resin sections for electron microscopy, not routine light-microscopy paraffin sections.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: types of microtome); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A muscle biopsy must be frozen for enzyme histochemistry. Why is it snap-frozen in isopentane chilled by liquid nitrogen instead of being dropped directly into liquid nitrogen?
options: Liquid nitrogen fixes and denatures the muscle enzymes
Isopentane penetrates and dehydrates the tissue before freezing
Liquid nitrogen is too cold for cryostat sectioning of muscle
A gas layer forms around the tissue and slows freezing
items.why: When warm tissue enters liquid nitrogen, the nitrogen boils and wraps the tissue in an insulating layer of gas. **This vapor layer slows heat transfer, so freezing is slow and ice-crystal artifact forms**. Isopentane cooled by liquid nitrogen stays liquid in contact with the tissue and freezes it rapidly and evenly.

whyNot.0: Freezing does not fix or denature enzymes; preserving enzyme activity is exactly why muscle is snap-frozen rather than fixed.
whyNot.1: Isopentane is used only as a cold heat-transfer liquid; it does not dehydrate or penetrate the tissue before freezing.
whyNot.2: The block is warmed to cryostat temperature before cutting anyway; the problem with liquid nitrogen is slow, uneven freezing, not its low temperature.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Frozen sections; enzyme histochemistry of muscle)

items.stem: A bone marrow trephine biopsy will be used for immunohistochemistry and molecular (DNA) testing. Which decalcifying agent is preferred to best preserve antigens and nucleic acids?
items.why: **EDTA is a chelating agent that binds calcium ions at near-neutral pH**, so it removes calcium gently. It is slow, but it gives the best preservation of morphology, antigens, and DNA and RNA.

whyNot.1: Nitric acid is a rapid strong-acid decalcifier, but it damages nuclear staining and degrades nucleic acids, making it a poor choice for molecular work.
whyNot.2: Hydrochloric acid is also a strong, fast acid that harms nuclear detail and nucleic acids if the exposure is not tightly controlled.
whyNot.3: Formic acid is a gentler weak acid and is widely used, but it still degrades DNA more than EDTA does, so it is not the preferred choice here.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Decalcification: chelating agents); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: How many mL of 95% ethanol are needed to prepare 500 mL of 70% ethanol by dilution with distilled water? (Ignore volume contraction on mixing.)
items.why: Use C1V1 = C2V2: (95%)(V1) = (70%)(500 mL), so V1 = 35,000 / 95 = **about 368 mL of 95% ethanol**, made up to 500 mL with water.

whyNot.0: About 132 mL is the volume of water to add (500 − 368), not the volume of 95% ethanol.
whyNot.1: 350 mL is 70% of 500 mL; it would be right only if the stock were 100% ethanol, which ignores that the stock is 95%.
whyNot.3: 475 mL is 95% of 500 mL; this inverts the formula by multiplying by the stock concentration instead of dividing by it.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: dehydration); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Laboratory solutions)

worked.problem: How many mL of absolute (100%) ethanol are needed to make 250 mL of 80% ethanol?
steps: Add water to a final volume of 250 mL (about 50 mL of water, ignoring contraction).
worked.result: 200 mL of absolute ethanol, diluted to 250 mL

items.stem: While a paraffin block is being trimmed, the knife strikes a small, unexpected calcified focus that the gross examination missed. What is the most appropriate way to obtain sections without reprocessing the whole specimen?
options: Soak the block face in ice water for an extended time, then re-cut
Re-cut with a smaller clearance angle and faster strokes
Briefly apply a weak acid to the block face, rinse, re-cut
Melt the block and re-embed the tissue in a harder paraffin
items.why: **Surface decalcification** treats only the exposed face of the block: it is placed in or on an acid decalcifier (e.g., about 1% hydrochloric acid) for a short time, rinsed, and re-cut. The acid penetrates only a short distance, enough to give a few good sections.

whyNot.0: Soaking in cold water softens and hydrates hard tissue slightly, but it cannot remove calcium salts.
whyNot.1: Changing the knife angle or cutting speed does not remove calcium; forcing the cut through it will tear the section and nick the knife.
whyNot.3: A harder wax does not dissolve calcium deposits, so the calcified focus would still tear sections and damage the knife.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Decalcification: surface decalcification); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Two serial sections of a liver biopsy are stained with PAS. In the untreated section, the hepatocytes are full of magenta granules; in the section treated with diastase before PAS, the granules are gone. The granules are most likely:
items.why: Diastase (or alpha-amylase) digests glycogen but leaves other PAS-positive materials untouched. **PAS-positive material that disappears after diastase digestion is glycogen**.

whyNot.1: Neutral mucins are PAS-positive and resist diastase, so they would still stain in the digested section.
whyNot.2: Alpha-1 antitrypsin globules in hepatocytes are characteristically PAS-positive and diastase-resistant, so they would persist after digestion.
whyNot.3: Fungal cell walls are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant, and would remain stained after digestion.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Carbohydrates: PAS and diastase digestion); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Golden-brown granules are seen in Kupffer cells in an H&E section of liver. Which special stain is used to show that they are hemosiderin, by staining ferric iron blue?
items.why: **Perls' Prussian blue reaction uses potassium ferrocyanide in dilute hydrochloric acid to form a blue ferric ferrocyanide precipitate** wherever ferric iron, as in hemosiderin, is present.

whyNot.0: Fontana-Masson is an argentaffin silver method used to demonstrate melanin, not iron.
whyNot.2: Von Kossa demonstrates calcium deposits (via their phosphate and carbonate) as black silver, not iron.
whyNot.3: Schmorl's ferric ferricyanide method stains reducing substances such as melanin and lipofuscin, not hemosiderin specifically.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Pigments and minerals: Perls' method); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A liver biopsy is stained with Masson's trichrome (aniline blue variant) to assess fibrosis. In a well-stained section, what color are the collagen fibers?
items.why: In Masson's trichrome, muscle and cytoplasm take up the red dye, and phosphomolybdic or phosphotungstic acid then lets the larger aniline blue molecules displace red from collagen. **Collagen stains blue** (or green with the light green variant), while nuclei are black.

whyNot.0: Red is the color of muscle and cytoplasm in Masson's trichrome; red collagen is the result in the Van Gieson method instead.
whyNot.1: Black is the color of nuclei (iron hematoxylin) in Masson's trichrome, and of elastic fibers in Verhoeff's stain.
whyNot.2: Yellow is the color of muscle and cytoplasm in the Van Gieson stain, which uses picric acid, not of collagen in Masson's.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Connective tissues and stains: Masson's trichrome); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: In the Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) method for fungi, which reagent oxidizes the cell wall polysaccharides to aldehydes that then reduce the silver solution?
items.why: **Chromic acid oxidizes polysaccharides in the fungal wall to aldehydes**, which reduce methenamine silver to black metallic silver. Fungi therefore appear black against a light green background.

whyNot.0: Sodium thiosulfate is used near the end to remove unreduced silver; it does not oxidize polysaccharides.
whyNot.2: Gold chloride is used for toning, which makes the silver deposit sharper and more stable; it plays no part in creating the aldehydes.
whyNot.3: Light green is the counterstain that colors the background green; it does not react with fungal walls.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microorganisms: Grocott methenamine silver); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Before immunohistochemical staining, sections from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue are heated in a citrate or EDTA buffer. What is the purpose of this step?
options: To unmask antigens hidden by formalin cross-links
To remove paraffin from the section
To block endogenous peroxidase activity in the tissue
To permanently attach the antibody to the tissue antigen
items.why: Formalin's methylene cross-links can mask the epitopes that antibodies recognize. **Heat-induced epitope retrieval in citrate or EDTA buffer breaks or loosens these cross-links and restores antigen reactivity**.

whyNot.2: Endogenous peroxidase is blocked with hydrogen peroxide (often in methanol), not with hot buffer.
whyNot.1: Paraffin is removed earlier with xylene and graded alcohols, before the sections are placed in the retrieval buffer.
whyNot.3: Antibody binding occurs during the antibody incubation steps after retrieval; the heating step does not bind antibody.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Immunohistochemical techniques: antigen retrieval)

items.stem: A 1 mL cerebrospinal fluid sample with very few cells is sent for cytology. Which preparation method concentrates the cells directly onto a small, defined area of a slide?
options: Direct smear of the uncentrifuged fluid
items.why: **A cytocentrifuge spins the fluid in a chamber against the slide**, depositing the cells in a small circle while filter paper absorbs the fluid. This makes it ideal for low-volume, low-cellularity fluids such as CSF.

whyNot.0: A cell block needs a visible sediment or clot to embed; a 1 mL low-cellularity CSF will rarely give enough material.
whyNot.1: A smear of uncentrifuged fluid spreads the few cells thinly over the slide, so they are easily missed.
whyNot.2: The Saccomanno technique is used for sputum, with pre-fixation and blending, not for CSF.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Diagnostic cytopathology: specimen preparation)

items.stem: The sediment from a large pleural effusion is clotted and processed into a paraffin cell block. What is the main advantage of this preparation over smears alone?
options: Many serial sections can be cut for special stains and IHC
It gives a faster result than conventional smears
It removes the need to fix the specimen
It shows nuclear detail better than an alcohol-fixed Pap smear
items.why: A cell block turns the cellular sediment into a paraffin block that is sectioned like tissue. **Its key advantage is that many serial sections can be cut for special stains and immunohistochemistry**, and small tissue fragments can be seen in their architectural context.

whyNot.1: A cell block takes longer than smears because it goes through fixation, processing, embedding, and sectioning.
whyNot.2: Cell blocks still need fixation (usually formalin) before processing; they do not avoid it.
whyNot.3: Alcohol-fixed, Pap-stained smears generally show finer nuclear detail; cell blocks are valued for ancillary studies and architecture rather than superior nuclear detail.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Diagnostic cytopathology: cell blocks)

items.stem: A specimen is collected into a fixative of about 50% ethanol containing polyethylene glycol (Carbowax), homogenized in a blender, concentrated by centrifugation, and then smeared. This Saccomanno technique is used for:
items.why: **The Saccomanno technique is a method for sputum**: pre-fixation in alcohol with polyethylene glycol and mechanical blending break up the mucus and spread diagnostic cells evenly, which improves the detection of lung cancer cells.

whyNot.0: Urine is usually concentrated by centrifugation, cytospin, filtration, or liquid-based methods; it is not mucoid and does not need blending.
whyNot.2: CSF is scant and fragile and is processed by cytocentrifugation; blending would destroy the few cells present.
whyNot.3: Fine-needle aspirates are smeared directly from the needle or rinsed into a liquid medium; they are not blended.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Diagnostic cytopathology: respiratory specimens)

items.stem: In an autopsy, the thoracic, cervical, abdominal, and pelvic organs are removed together as one mass and then dissected outside the body. This method of evisceration is credited to:
items.why: **The Letulle method removes all the organs en masse** as one unit, preserving the connections between organ systems for later dissection. It is fast at the table but leaves a large, unwieldy organ mass to dissect.

whyNot.0: The Virchow method removes the organs one by one and examines each separately.
whyNot.1: The Rokitansky method dissects the organs largely in situ, with little removal before examination.
whyNot.2: The Ghon method removes the organs en bloc as several functional blocks (e.g., thoracic, abdominal, urogenital), not as a single mass.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Autopsy); Ludwig J, Handbook of Autopsy Practice

items.stem: In a histopathology quality assurance program, errors are classified by the phase of the testing process in which they occur. Which of the following is a pre-analytical error?
options: H&E sections that are too pale because the hematoxylin was exhausted
A biopsy left in saline overnight before it was placed in formalin
A correct diagnosis typed into the wrong patient's report
A tissue fragment from another case picked up from the water bath
items.why: Pre-analytical errors occur before the specimen is processed and examined, from collection to delivery to the lab. **Delayed fixation (a biopsy left in saline) is a pre-analytical error** that causes autolysis and can affect special stains and IHC.

whyNot.0: Weak hematoxylin staining happens during processing and staining in the laboratory, so it is an analytical error.
whyNot.2: A transcription error in the report occurs after the diagnosis is made, so it is a post-analytical error.
whyNot.3: A floater picked up from the water bath arises during sectioning in the lab, making it an analytical error.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Quality management in histopathology); CLSI QMS01, Quality Management System: A Model for Laboratory Services

items.stem: Under Section 21 of RA 5527, as amended by RA 6138 and PD 498, a certificate of registration as a medical technologist shall not be issued to a successful examinee who has not yet reached what age?
items.why: Section 21, as amended, provides that no certificate shall be issued to any successful applicant **who has not attained the age of twenty-one (21) years**. A candidate may pass the examination earlier but must wait until 21 to be registered.

whyNot.0: Eighteen is the general age of majority in the Philippines, but the Act sets a higher minimum for issuing the certificate.
whyNot.1: Twenty years does not appear in Section 21; the statutory minimum is twenty-one.
whyNot.3: Twenty-five years is not the requirement; the Act sets the minimum at twenty-one.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 21, as amended by RA 6138 (1970) and PD 498 (1974)

items.stem: Under Section 23 of RA 5527, which of the following is a ground on which the Board shall refuse to issue a certificate of registration?
options: Lacking the CPD units required for license renewal
Having a general average below 80% in the board exam
Being guilty of immoral or dishonorable conduct
Not yet being employed in a licensed clinical laboratory
items.why: Section 23 directs the Board to refuse registration to any person convicted by a court of competent jurisdiction of a criminal offense involving moral turpitude, **any person guilty of immoral or dishonorable conduct**, or anyone of unsound mind or with an incurable communicable disease. The Board must give its reasons in writing.

whyNot.0: CPD units are a requirement for renewing the Professional Identification Card under RA 10912, not a ground for refusing initial registration under Section 23.
whyNot.1: Passing requires a general average of at least 75% (Section 19), so a rating below 80% is not a reason to refuse a certificate.
whyNot.3: Employment is not a condition for registration; Section 23 lists only conviction, immoral or dishonorable conduct, unsound mind, and incurable communicable disease.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 23

items.stem: Under Section 14 of RA 5527, which of the following persons may perform the work of medical technology in the Philippines without a certificate of registration from the Board?
options: A BSMT graduate who is awaiting the release of board exam results
A foreign medical technologist hired as regular staff of a private hospital
A licensed nurse who has completed in-house laboratory training
items.why: Section 14 prohibits anyone from practicing medical technology without a valid certificate of registration, but exempts **duly registered physicians**. The other exemptions are foreign medical technologists called in for consultation or as visiting or exchange professors, and those serving only the United States Armed Forces stationed in the Philippines.

whyNot.0: A graduate who has not yet passed and registered has no certificate, and Section 14 gives no exemption for examinees awaiting results.
whyNot.1: Foreign medical technologists are exempt only when called in for consultation or as visiting or exchange professors, not when employed as regular hospital staff.
whyNot.2: Holding a nursing license does not exempt a person from Section 14; in-house training is not a substitute for registration as a medical technologist.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 14

items.stem: A hospital laboratory processes specimens in order of clinical urgency, never according to the patient's ability to pay, social standing, or personal connections with the staff. Which bioethical principle does this policy most directly uphold?
items.why: **Justice requires fair and equitable treatment, including the fair distribution of services** according to need rather than wealth or status. Prioritizing by clinical urgency alone applies this principle.

whyNot.1: Autonomy concerns a competent patient's right to make decisions about his or her own care, not how services are distributed among patients.
whyNot.2: Fidelity is faithfulness to commitments and duties owed to patients, such as keeping promises; it is not mainly about fair allocation.
whyNot.3: Veracity is the duty to tell the truth, which is not what this triage policy addresses.

items.ref: Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics

items.stem: Bioethicists separate the duty not to inflict harm on others from the duty to act positively for others' benefit, such as preventing or removing harm. The duty not to inflict harm is called:
items.why: **Non-maleficence is the obligation to refrain from causing harm** ("first, do no harm"). Beneficence is the separate, positive duty to act for the patient's good, including preventing and removing harm.

whyNot.0: Beneficence is the positive duty to do good and to prevent or remove harm, which the stem describes as the second, separate duty.
whyNot.1: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of benefits, burdens, and resources, not the duty to avoid harming an individual.
whyNot.3: Autonomy is respect for a competent person's right to self-determination, not a duty to avoid harm.

items.ref: Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics

items.stem: A laboratory plans to buy a new automated tissue processor that is expected to be used for about ten years. In the laboratory budget, this purchase is classified as a:
items.why: **Equipment with a long useful life and a cost above the institution's threshold is a capital expenditure**, budgeted separately from day-to-day costs and usually depreciated over its useful life.

whyNot.0: The operating budget covers recurring day-to-day costs such as reagents, supplies, and maintenance contracts, not long-lived equipment.
whyNot.2: Personnel costs are salaries, wages, and benefits of staff, not equipment purchases.
whyNot.3: Revenue is income the laboratory earns from test charges; a purchase is an expenditure, not revenue.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Financial management)

items.stem: To shorten turnaround time, a histopathology section tries a new specimen-batching schedule for one month, then compares the turnaround data with the baseline to see if it improved. In the PDCA (Deming) cycle, this comparison is the:
items.why: In the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle, the change is planned, tried on a small scale (Do), and then evaluated. **The Check (or Study) step measures the results of the trial against the baseline or target**, which leads to the Act step.

whyNot.0: The Plan step identifies the problem and designs the change; it comes before any trial data exist.
whyNot.1: The Do step is carrying out the one-month trial itself, not analyzing its results.
whyNot.3: The Act step comes after the check: the change is adopted, standardized, or abandoned based on the results.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Quality management); CLSI QMS01

items.stem: A laboratory bench must be covered by one medical technologist 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. If 1 FTE equals 2,080 paid hours per year and leave is ignored, how many FTEs are needed for this one position?
items.why: Hours to cover = 24 h × 365 days = 8,760 h per year. Divide by 2,080 h per FTE: 8,760 / 2,080 = **about 4.2 FTEs**. Real staffing needs are even higher once leave and other non-productive hours are added.

whyNot.0: A single round-the-clock position is not the same as one FTE; one person working 2,080 hours covers less than a quarter of the year's hours.
whyNot.1: 1.4 FTE covers only one 8-hour shift every day (8 × 365 / 2,080), not the full 24 hours.
whyNot.2: 3.0 FTE assumes one person per shift, but each person works only about 40 hours a week, so three people cannot cover all 168 hours each week.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Staffing and productivity)

worked.problem: A section is staffed by one person 16 hours a day, 7 days a week, all year. If 1 FTE = 2,080 paid hours per year (leave ignored), how many FTEs are needed?
steps: Annual hours to cover = 16 h × 365 days = 5,840 h

items.stem: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa are seen in measles and essentially no other disease, so finding them practically establishes the diagnosis. A finding that is characteristic of one particular disease in this way is described as:
items.why: A sign or finding that occurs in only one disease, and therefore identifies it, is **pathognomonic**. Koplik spots are the classic example for measles. Most signs are nonspecific and must be interpreted together with other findings.

whyNot.1: A prodrome is the early, nonspecific phase of illness before the characteristic features appear; it describes timing, not diagnostic specificity.
whyNot.2: Idiopathic means the cause of a disease is unknown, which says nothing about how specific a sign is.
whyNot.3: Subclinical refers to disease that produces no detectable signs or symptoms, the opposite of a distinctive visible finding.

items.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary

items.stem: Hypoxia from severe anemia and ischemia from a blocked artery both deprive cells of oxygen, yet ischemia usually injures tissue faster and more severely. What is the main reason?
options: Anemic blood still carries a normal amount of oxygen to the tissues
Ischemia causes cells to undergo apoptosis instead of necrosis
Ischemia also stops glucose delivery and the removal of wastes
Ischemic injury is driven mainly by bacteria entering the dead tissue
items.why: In hypoxia with preserved blood flow, cells can still generate some ATP by anaerobic glycolysis using glucose delivered by the blood. In ischemia, **blood flow stops, so glycolytic substrates are no longer supplied and accumulating metabolites are not washed out**, which halts even anaerobic energy production. Injury therefore develops faster and is more severe.

whyNot.0: Anemia lowers the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, so it does reduce oxygen delivery; that is why it causes hypoxia.
whyNot.1: Severe ischemia typically produces necrosis (for example, coagulative necrosis in an infarct); the type of cell death does not explain the greater severity.
whyNot.3: Infection is not the mechanism of ischemic injury; the damage comes from loss of blood flow itself.

items.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (Cell injury: causes; hypoxia and ischemia)

items.stem: A patient complains of nausea and a throbbing headache. On examination, the physician records a temperature of 39 °C and palpates an enlarged liver. Which of the following is a symptom rather than a sign?
options: The temperature of 39 °C measured with a thermometer
The enlarged liver felt on palpation
Yellow discoloration of the sclera seen by the examiner
items.why: A symptom is a **subjective experience reported by the patient**, such as pain, nausea, or headache. A sign is an objective finding that an examiner can observe or measure, such as fever on a thermometer, hepatomegaly, or jaundice.

whyNot.0: A measured fever is an objective finding that the examiner can verify, so it is a sign.
whyNot.1: Hepatomegaly found by the examiner on physical examination is an objective sign.
whyNot.2: Jaundice observed by the examiner is an objective, visible sign.

items.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; Dorland's Illustrated Medical Dictionary

items.stem: In a long-term cigarette smoker, patches of the normal ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium of the bronchi are replaced by stratified squamous epithelium without cellular atypia. This change is called:
items.why: Metaplasia is a reversible change in which one differentiated adult cell type is replaced by another that is better able to withstand stress. **Columnar-to-squamous metaplasia in the airways of smokers** is the classic example. The squamous epithelium is tougher but loses mucus secretion and ciliary clearance.

whyNot.0: Dysplasia means disordered growth with cellular atypia (pleomorphism, loss of orientation); the stem states there is no atypia.
whyNot.2: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells of the same type, not replacement by a different epithelium.
whyNot.3: Atrophy is shrinkage in cell size or number; it does not change one epithelial type into another.

items.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease (Cellular adaptations: metaplasia)

items.stem: A tophus is removed from a patient with suspected gout, and the pathologist wants the urate crystals preserved in the sections. Which fixative should be used?
items.why: Monosodium urate crystals are **soluble in water**, so they are lost in aqueous fixatives such as formalin. Fixing the specimen in absolute (non-aqueous) alcohol keeps the crystals, which can then be seen as needle-shaped, birefringent structures under polarized light.

whyNot.0: Formalin is an aqueous solution, and the water-soluble urate crystals dissolve out during fixation.
whyNot.1: Bouin's fluid is aqueous and acidic, so it also dissolves the urate crystals.
whyNot.2: Zenker's fluid is an aqueous mercuric-dichromate mixture; it does not preserve water-soluble urates.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Pigments and minerals: urates); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A 2 cm³ piece of tissue is to be fixed by immersion in 10% neutral buffered formalin. About how much fixative should be used relative to the tissue volume?
options: About equal to the tissue volume
items.why: Fixative is consumed as it reacts with the tissue, so a generous excess is needed for complete fixation. Standard texts recommend **about 15 to 20 times the tissue volume** of fixative (Bruce-Gregorios gives a range of 10 to 25 times). Too small a volume leads to under-fixation, especially in the center of the specimen.

whyNot.0: An equal volume is quickly diluted and exhausted by the tissue, leaving the center poorly fixed.
whyNot.1: Twice the volume is still far too little; the fixative becomes depleted before fixation is complete.
whyNot.3: There is no benefit to such a large excess; it wastes reagent and creates more hazardous waste without improving fixation.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: practical considerations); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: An ingredient found in both Bouin's fluid and Carnoy's fluid lyses red blood cells, so these fixatives are poor choices when erythrocytes must be preserved. Which ingredient is this?
items.why: Bouin's fluid contains picric acid, formalin, and glacial acetic acid, while Carnoy's contains ethanol, chloroform, and glacial acetic acid. **Acetic acid lyses red blood cells** and swells collagen, which is why it is often added to offset shrinkage. Fixatives containing it are avoided when red cells need to be preserved.

whyNot.0: Picric acid is in Bouin's fluid but not in Carnoy's fluid (ethanol, chloroform, acetic acid), so it is not the shared ingredient.
whyNot.2: Mercuric chloride is found in Zenker's and B5 fluids, not in Bouin's or Carnoy's.
whyNot.3: Potassium dichromate is a component of Zenker's, Helly's, and Orth's fluids, not Bouin's or Carnoy's.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: acetic acid, Bouin's and Carnoy's fluids); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: To check decalcification chemically, a sample of the used acid decalcifying fluid is made neutral to alkaline with ammonium hydroxide, and saturated ammonium oxalate is then added. The fluid turns cloudy with a white precipitate. What should the technologist do?
options: Continue decalcifying in fresh fluid and repeat the test later
Stop decalcification, since the specimen is now ready
Wash the tissue and process it, since cloudiness means the acid is spent
Discard the specimen, since the precipitate means it was over-decalcified
items.why: The ammonium oxalate test detects calcium released into the decalcifying fluid as a white calcium oxalate precipitate. **A precipitate means calcium is still present**, so decalcification is incomplete; the specimen is placed in fresh fluid and the test is repeated until the sample stays clear.

whyNot.1: A precipitate shows that calcium is still being removed from the tissue, so the end point has not been reached.
whyNot.2: Cloudiness indicates dissolved calcium, not exhausted acid alone; processing now would leave calcified areas that tear the sections.
whyNot.3: Over-decalcification cannot be detected this way; the test only shows whether calcium is still coming out of the tissue.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Decalcification: chemical end-point test); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Paraffin ribbons are floated on a water bath to flatten them before they are picked up on slides. If the paraffin melts at 56 °C, which bath temperature is most appropriate?
items.why: The flotation bath should be **slightly below the melting point of the paraffin** (roughly 6 to 10 °C below). This softens the wax enough for the section to spread flat without melting it.

whyNot.0: Water at room temperature is too cool to soften the wax, so folds and wrinkles in the sections will not flatten out.
whyNot.2: This is above the wax's melting point; the paraffin melts and the section breaks apart and disperses on the water.
whyNot.3: This is well above the melting point, so the section would melt and the tissue could also be damaged by the heat.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: floating out sections); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A reusable steel microtome knife has small nicks visible along its cutting edge. Which sharpening step is meant to remove these nicks?
options: Increasing the clearance angle on the microtome
items.why: Knife sharpening has two stages. **Honing on an abrasive stone removes nicks and irregularities** and restores the edge. Stropping on leather then removes the burr left by honing and polishes the edge.

whyNot.0: Stropping removes the fine burr and polishes the edge after honing; it cannot grind away nicks.
whyNot.1: Xylene only cleans off wax and debris; it has no abrasive action on the steel.
whyNot.2: The clearance angle affects how the knife meets the block; it does not repair a damaged edge.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Microtome knives: honing and stropping); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy)

items.stem: Which processing reagent can serve as both dehydrating and clearing agent, because it mixes with water, alcohol, and melted paraffin, but is now rarely used because of its toxicity?
items.why: **Dioxane mixes with water, alcohol, and paraffin**, so tissue can go from water to dioxane and then directly into paraffin, skipping a separate clearing step. Its toxicity, especially with repeated exposure, has made it largely obsolete in routine laboratories.

whyNot.0: Xylene is a clearing agent but does not mix with water, so tissue must be fully dehydrated before it goes into xylene.
whyNot.1: Acetone is a fast dehydrating agent, but it is not used as a clearing agent for paraffin infiltration.
whyNot.3: Chloroform is a clearing agent that mixes with paraffin, but it does not mix with water and cannot dehydrate tissue.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Dehydration and clearing: dioxane); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing)

items.stem: A frozen section stained with Oil Red O for fat must be mounted in an aqueous medium such as glycerin jelly instead of a resinous mountant. Why?
options: The alcohol and xylene steps would dissolve the lipid
Resinous mountants have a refractive index too far from that of glass
Aqueous mountants set hard faster, preventing fading of the dye
Glycerin chemically intensifies the red color of Oil Red O
items.why: Mounting in a resinous medium requires dehydration through alcohols and clearing in xylene, and **these organic solvents would dissolve the lipid** along with the dye. An aqueous medium lets the section go straight from water to coverslip, so the stained fat is kept.

whyNot.1: Synthetic resin mountants are chosen precisely because their refractive index is close to that of glass.
whyNot.2: Aqueous mountants are generally slower to set; speed is not the reason they are chosen here.
whyNot.3: Glycerin does not react with the dye; it simply provides a mounting medium free of lipid solvents.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Lipids: Oil Red O; Mounting media); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Serial paraffin sections come off the microtome in a repeating pattern: one thick, the next thin, then thick again. Which fault should be checked first?
options: There is a nick in the knife edge
The paraffin is too soft for the room temperature
The block or knife is loose in its holder
items.why: When the block holder or knife clamp is loose, **the block or knife shifts slightly with each stroke**, so successive sections come out thick and thin. Other causes include an inadequate clearance angle and a worn advance mechanism; tightening the clamps is the first thing to check.

whyNot.0: A nick produces a vertical score or split line through each section, not alternating thickness.
whyNot.1: Wax that is too soft causes the sections to compress and crumble, not to alternate in thickness.
whyNot.3: Incomplete dehydration causes poor infiltration and crumbling or mushy tissue, not a regular thick-thin pattern.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: section faults and remedies); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: Two L-shaped brass or metal pieces are set on a flat metal plate and slid together to form a rectangular mold whose size can be adjusted to fit the tissue. This embedding mold is known as:
options: A Tissue-Tek base mold with cassette
items.why: **Leuckhart's embedding mold consists of two L-shaped metal pieces** resting on a metal base plate. Moving the L-pieces adjusts the size of the mold to suit the specimen. It is one of the traditional, reusable embedding molds.

whyNot.0: Peel-away molds are single-use plastic molds with fixed sizes whose sides are peeled off after the wax hardens.
whyNot.2: This system uses a stainless steel or plastic base mold topped by a plastic cassette that becomes the block holder, not L-shaped pieces.
whyNot.3: Ice-tray molds are disposable multi-compartment trays used to embed several specimens, not adjustable L-pieces.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Embedding: types of blocking-out molds)

items.stem: At a cryostat setting that gives excellent sections of liver, sections from a fatty breast specimen crumble and smear. Which adjustment is most likely to help?
options: Fix the tissue in formalin before freezing it
Cut thinner sections, at about 1 µm
Lower the specimen temperature (make it colder)
items.why: Fat has a lower freezing point than most tissues, so it may not be hard enough at a setting suited to liver or brain. **Fatty tissue needs a colder cryostat temperature** (often in the range of −25 to −35 °C) to cut cleanly.

whyNot.0: Warmer settings make fatty tissue even softer and more likely to smear; fat needs colder, not warmer, temperatures.
whyNot.1: Formalin fixation does not solidify the lipid, and for intraoperative frozen sections it would also cause unacceptable delay.
whyNot.2: Cutting thinner does not solve the problem of fat that is not frozen hard; fatty frozen sections are, if anything, cut slightly thicker.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Frozen sections: cryostat temperatures for different tissues)

items.stem: A section stained by the Van Gieson method (picric acid and acid fuchsin) is examined. What colors are expected for collagen and for smooth muscle?
items.why: In the Van Gieson method, the larger acid fuchsin molecules bind collagen, while the small picric acid molecules stain the more compact muscle and cytoplasm. **Collagen is red and muscle, cytoplasm, and red cells are yellow.**

whyNot.1: These are the colors of Masson's trichrome with aniline blue, not Van Gieson.
whyNot.2: Black fibers are typical of silver impregnation methods such as reticulin stains, not Van Gieson.
whyNot.3: This reverses the result: the acid fuchsin stains collagen, and picric acid stains muscle and cytoplasm.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Connective tissues: Van Gieson method); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A spinal cord section is examined for loss of myelin in a suspected demyelinating disease. Which stain is used specifically to demonstrate myelin?
items.why: **Luxol fast blue is the standard stain for myelin**, which it colors blue to blue-green. It is often combined with cresyl violet or PAS, and areas of demyelination appear pale.

whyNot.0: Congo red demonstrates amyloid, which shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
whyNot.1: Mucicarmine stains epithelial mucins and the capsule of Cryptococcus, not myelin.
whyNot.3: Gordon and Sweet is a silver method for reticulin fibers, not for myelin sheaths.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Neuropathological techniques: myelin stains); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: In the Fontana–Masson method, melanin reduces ammoniacal silver to black metallic silver without any added reducing agent. Substances with this property are described as:
items.why: **Argentaffin substances can reduce silver solutions on their own**, while argyrophil substances need a separate reducing step. Melanin and the granules of some neuroendocrine cells are argentaffin, which is the basis of the Fontana–Masson stain.

whyNot.0: Argyrophil substances take up silver but need an external reducing agent to convert it to visible metallic silver.
whyNot.2: Metachromasia is staining in a color different from the dye's own color (e.g., mast cells with toluidine blue), not silver reduction.
whyNot.3: Birefringence is double refraction of polarized light, a property of crystals and amyloid stained with Congo red.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Pigments and minerals: melanin, Fontana-Masson); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques

items.stem: A fresh pleural fluid for cytology arrives late in the evening and cannot be processed until the next morning. What is the best way to hold it overnight?
options: Add an equal volume of 10% formalin
items.why: Fresh body fluids are protein-rich and the cells stay reasonably well preserved for a short time if cold. **Refrigeration at about 4 °C slows degeneration** and is the standard way to hold an unprocessed fluid; it should still be processed as soon as possible.

whyNot.1: Body temperature speeds autolysis and bacterial growth, so the cells degenerate faster.
whyNot.2: Freezing forms ice crystals that rupture the cells and destroy morphology.
whyNot.3: Formalin-fixed cells stain poorly with the Papanicolaou method, so formalin is not the routine way to hold cytology fluids.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Diagnostic cytopathology: serous fluids, specimen handling)

items.stem: For urine cytology to detect urothelial carcinoma, why is the first-voided morning urine usually avoided?
options: It contains too few cells to make a slide
It is too dilute to centrifuge effectively
