It is always contaminated with vaginal or skin cells
Cells held in the bladder overnight have degenerated
items.why: Urine is a hostile medium for cells, and those sitting in the bladder overnight show **degenerative changes that make interpretation difficult**. A fresh voided specimen from later in the morning (not the first one), or a bladder washing, gives better-preserved cells.

whyNot.0: The overnight specimen is often cellular; the problem is the poor preservation of those cells, not their number.
whyNot.1: First morning urine is usually the most concentrated sample of the day, not the most dilute.
whyNot.2: Contamination depends on collection technique, not on the time of day the sample is passed.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Diagnostic cytopathology: urine specimens)

items.stem: Compared with a conventional Papanicolaou smear, what is a main advantage of liquid-based cervical cytology?
options: No fixative is needed for the specimen
Slides no longer need screening by a cytotechnologist
A thin, even cell layer with less blood and mucus
A lower cost per test than a conventional smear
items.why: In liquid-based cytology, the sampling device is rinsed into a vial of preservative, and the processor removes much of the blood, mucus, and inflammatory debris. The result is **a thin, evenly distributed layer of well-fixed cells**, which reduces unsatisfactory slides and makes screening easier.

whyNot.0: Liquid-based cytology vials contain a preservative fixative; the cells are fixed immediately in it.
whyNot.1: The slides still have to be screened and interpreted; only the slide preparation is changed.
whyNot.3: Liquid-based cytology generally costs more because of the special vials, reagents, and processors.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Diagnostic cytopathology: liquid-based cytology)

items.stem: According to The Bethesda System for Reporting Cervical Cytology, what is the minimum estimated number of well-visualized, well-preserved squamous cells for a liquid-based preparation to be satisfactory?
items.why: The Bethesda System sets a minimum squamous cellularity of about 8,000 to 12,000 cells for conventional smears and **at least 5,000 cells for liquid-based preparations**. Specimens below these numbers are reported as unsatisfactory for evaluation.

whyNot.0: Five hundred cells is far below the threshold; such a slide would be reported as unsatisfactory for evaluation.
whyNot.2: Two thousand cells is still below the minimum and would not be considered adequate.
whyNot.3: This is higher than required; the conventional smear threshold is 8,000 to 12,000 cells, and the liquid-based threshold is lower.

items.ref: Nayar R, Wilbur DC (eds.), The Bethesda System for Reporting Cervical Cytology, 3rd ed. (Specimen adequacy)

items.stem: Several fine-needle aspiration smears of a lymph node were allowed to air-dry before they reached the laboratory. Which stain is best suited to these smears?
items.why: Romanowsky stains such as May-Grünwald-Giemsa or Diff-Quik are **meant for air-dried smears** and show cytoplasm, granules, and background material well. The Papanicolaou stain needs immediate wet fixation, so air-dried smears are poorly suited to it.

whyNot.0: The Pap stain is designed for wet-fixed smears; air-drying causes swollen, pale nuclei and loss of detail with this stain.
whyNot.1: Mucicarmine is a special stain for epithelial mucin, not a routine stain for assessing cell morphology.
whyNot.2: Ziehl–Neelsen is a special stain for acid-fast bacilli, not a general morphological stain.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Diagnostic cytopathology: fixation and staining of smears)

items.stem: A known amyloid-containing tissue is stained as a control with each Congo red run. When the control is examined under polarized light, which finding shows that the run is valid?
options: Apple-green birefringence of the amyloid deposits
Bright blue fluorescence of the deposits
Black granular deposits in the amyloid
Uniform orange-red staining with no birefringence
items.why: With Congo red, amyloid stains orange-red in ordinary light and shows **apple-green birefringence under polarized light**. A positive control that gives this result shows that the reagents and procedure worked, so a negative patient slide can be trusted.

whyNot.1: Blue fluorescence is not the expected Congo red result; the stain is judged by its color under polarized light.
whyNot.2: Black deposits are typical of silver methods, not of a Congo red stain.
whyNot.3: Orange-red staining without birefringence is not specific for amyloid; the control has failed if birefringence is absent.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Amyloid: Congo red; Quality control in histopathology)

items.stem: To keep fragments of one patient's tissue from appearing on another patient's slide, what should the technologist do between blocks when floating out sections?
options: Add more adhesive to the water bath
Trim the next block more deeply
Clear the water bath surface of debris
items.why: Pieces of tissue left on the water bath can be picked up with the next patient's section and appear as a contaminant (a "floater"). **Clearing the water surface between blocks**, for example by drawing tissue paper across it, prevents this carryover.

whyNot.0: A hotter bath would melt the wax and does nothing to remove fragments left from the previous block.
whyNot.1: Adhesive helps sections stick to slides; it would make stray fragments more likely to adhere, not less.
whyNot.2: Trimming affects the block being cut, not fragments already floating on the water.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: floating out; Quality management in histopathology)

items.stem: As part of quality assurance, a laboratory routinely compares each intraoperative frozen section diagnosis with the final diagnosis on permanent paraffin sections and reviews any discrepancies. What does this activity mainly monitor?
options: Precision of the cryostat's section thickness setting
Diagnostic accuracy of the frozen section service
Turnaround time of routine paraffin processing
items.why: Frozen section to permanent section correlation is a standard quality assurance indicator. It **measures how often the rapid intraoperative diagnosis agrees with the final diagnosis**, and review of discrepancies (for example, sampling or interpretation errors) is used to improve the service.

whyNot.0: Section thickness is a matter of instrument performance and is checked separately; it is not what a diagnostic comparison measures.
whyNot.2: Turnaround time is measured with time-stamps, not by comparing diagnoses.
whyNot.3: Reagent performance is checked with control slides, not by frozen-permanent correlation.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Quality management in histopathology); CAP Laboratory Accreditation Program, Anatomic Pathology Checklist

items.stem: Under Section 17 of RA 5527 as amended by PD 498, which of the following board examination subjects carries a weight of 10% rather than 20%?
items.why: Section 17 gives 20% each to Clinical Chemistry, Microbiology and Parasitology, Hematology, and Blood Banking and Serology. **Clinical Microscopy (urinalysis and other body fluids) carries 10%**, the same weight as the subject covering histopathologic techniques, cytotechnology, MT laws, and ethics.

whyNot.0: Clinical Chemistry carries 20% under Section 17.
whyNot.1: Hematology carries 20% under Section 17.
whyNot.3: Blood Banking and Serology carries 20% under Section 17.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 17, as amended by PD 498 (1974)

items.stem: Under Section 19 of RA 5527, what must a BS Medical Technology graduate who has failed the medical technology board examination three times complete before being allowed to take it again?
options: 12 months of refresher course or postgraduate training
A 6-month review program in an accredited review center
A 3-year waiting period, with no further training required
Nothing, because the applicant is permanently disqualified
items.why: Section 19 provides that no further examination will be given to an applicant who has not qualified after three examinations until **12 months of refresher course in an accredited medical technology school or 12 months of postgraduate training in an accredited laboratory** has been completed.

whyNot.1: Section 19 sets a 12-month period and specifies an accredited school or laboratory, not a review center.
whyNot.2: Section 19 sets no waiting period; it requires further training before another attempt.
whyNot.3: For a BS Medical Technology graduate the Act allows a further attempt once the required training is done; only graduates of other paramedical professions are barred after a third failure.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 19

items.stem: A medical technologist's certificate of registration was revoked by the Board. Under Section 26 of RA 5527, what does the law provide about getting it back?
options: It is automatically restored two years after revocation
It can be restored only by passing the board examination again
It can never be reissued once it has been revoked
The Board may reissue it upon application
items.why: Section 26 (Reinstatement) states that the Board may, **upon application and for reason deemed proper and sufficient, reissue any revoked registration certificate**. Reinstatement is therefore discretionary, not automatic.

whyNot.0: Section 26 sets no automatic restoration and no fixed waiting period; reissuance is at the Board's discretion on application.
whyNot.1: Section 26 does not require a new examination; the Board may simply reissue the revoked certificate.
whyNot.2: Section 26 expressly allows the Board to reissue a revoked certificate.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 26

items.stem: A person who is not registered practices medical technology for a fee. Under Section 29 of RA 5527, what is the penalty upon conviction?
options: Fine of ₱500–₱1,000 only, with no imprisonment
₱2,000–₱5,000 fine or 6 months–2 years prison, or both
Fine of ₱2,000–₱5,000 only, with no imprisonment
Imprisonment of 6–12 years with no option of a fine
items.why: Section 29 punishes violations, including practicing without a certificate of registration, by **a fine of not less than ₱2,000 nor more than ₱5,000, or imprisonment of not less than six months nor more than two years, or both**, in the discretion of the court.

whyNot.0: The amounts are too low, and Section 29 provides for imprisonment as well as a fine.
whyNot.2: The fine range is correct, but Section 29 also allows imprisonment, or both penalties, at the court's discretion.
whyNot.3: These are not the penalties in Section 29, which allows a fine as an alternative to imprisonment.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 29

items.stem: Parents decline newborn screening for their baby because of their religious beliefs. Under the Newborn Screening Act of 2004 (RA 9288), what must happen?
options: Parents sign a written acknowledgment kept in the record
Screening is done anyway, since the Act does not allow refusal
The hospital must get a court order before discharging the baby
A verbal refusal is accepted, and nothing needs to be documented
items.why: Section 7 allows a parent or legal guardian to refuse testing on the grounds of religious beliefs, but they must **acknowledge in writing that refusal places the newborn at risk** for undiagnosed heritable conditions. A copy goes into the newborn's medical record, and the refusal is indicated in the national newborn screening database.

whyNot.1: Section 7 expressly allows parents or guardians to refuse on the grounds of religious beliefs.
whyNot.2: The Act requires documentation of the refusal, not a court order.
whyNot.3: The refusal must be acknowledged in writing and recorded; a verbal refusal alone is not enough.

items.ref: RA 9288 Sec. 7

items.stem: Under the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173), a patient's laboratory results stored in a hospital information system are classified as:
options: Public information, because it is held by a hospital
Non-personal data, because they are only numbers
items.why: Section 3(l) of RA 10173 defines sensitive personal information to include information about an individual's **health**, along with items such as genetic data, age, and government-issued identifiers. Its processing is generally prohibited except in the cases allowed by the Act, such as for medical treatment.

whyNot.0: Information about an individual's health is placed in the higher, sensitive category, not ordinary personal information.
whyNot.1: Being held by a hospital does not make health data public; it remains protected personal data.
whyNot.3: Results linked to an identifiable patient are personal data, whatever form they take.

items.ref: RA 10173 Sec. 3(l), Sec. 13

items.stem: Under the PRC Modernization Act of 2000 (RA 8981), within what period must a Professional Regulatory Board submit the signed results of a licensure examination to the Commission?
options: Within 30 days from the last day of the examination
Within 60 days from the last day of the examination
Within 120 days from the last day of the examination
Within 10 days from the last day of the examination
items.why: Section 9(h) of RA 8981 requires each Board to submit the results in all subjects, duly signed by its members, to the Commission **within ten (10) days from the last day of examination**, unless the Commission extends this for justifiable cause.

whyNot.0: Thirty days is not the period in RA 8981; the Act sets a much shorter deadline.
whyNot.1: Sixty days is not stated in RA 8981; the Board must submit results within 10 days unless extended.
whyNot.2: 120 days was the period in the original Section 18 of RA 5527 for reporting results to the Commissioner of Civil Service, not the RA 8981 deadline.

items.ref: RA 8981 Sec. 9(h); compare RA 5527 Sec. 18

items.stem: Each regulated profession has its own CPD Council that accredits CPD providers and programs. According to RA 10912, who chairs this council?
options: A PRB member chosen by that Board
The president of the accredited professional organization (APO)
The Chairperson of the Professional Regulation Commission
The president of the national organization of deans
items.why: Section 7 of RA 10912 makes **a member of the Professional Regulatory Board, chosen by that Board, the Chairperson** of the CPD Council. The other two members are the president or authorized officer of the APO and the president or officer of the national organization of deans or department chairpersons.

whyNot.1: The APO president or authorized officer sits on the CPD Council as its first member, not as its Chairperson.
whyNot.2: The PRC Chairperson is not named as head of the individual CPD Councils under Section 7.
whyNot.3: The president of the national organization of deans or department chairpersons is the second member, not the Chairperson.

items.ref: RA 10912 Sec. 7

items.stem: A patient's sister phones the laboratory and asks for the patient's test results, saying the family needs to know. The medical technologist politely declines and refers her to the patient and attending physician. Which ethical duty is the technologist upholding?
items.why: A patient's laboratory results are confidential and are released only to the patient, the requesting physician, or others the patient has authorized. **Refusing to disclose results to a relative without authorization upholds confidentiality.** Referring the caller to the proper source avoids both a breach and unhelpfulness.

whyNot.0: Beneficence is the duty to act for the patient's benefit; withholding results from a relative is mainly about protecting private information.
whyNot.2: Justice concerns fair distribution of resources and equal treatment, not who may receive a patient's results.
whyNot.3: Veracity is the duty to tell the truth; the technologist is not being asked to be truthful or deceptive here.

items.ref: Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics; PAMET Code of Ethics

items.stem: A clinic patient signs a consent form for a research blood draw after being told that refusing would mean losing her free follow-up care at the clinic. Which element of valid informed consent is missing?
items.why: Valid informed consent requires competence, disclosure, comprehension, voluntariness, and the consent itself. **Threatening to withdraw care if she refuses is coercion**, so her consent is not voluntary even though it was signed.

whyNot.1: The stem does not say she was denied information about the study; the problem is the pressure placed on her decision.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests she lacks the capacity to make decisions; she is an adult clinic patient.
whyNot.3: The stem gives no sign that she misunderstood the study; she was pressured, not confused.

items.ref: Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics (Informed consent); National Ethical Guidelines for Health and Health-Related Research (PHREB)

items.stem: In one month, a laboratory spends ₱45,000 on reagents and supplies, ₱30,000 on labor, and ₱15,000 on allocated overhead for a test, and performs 1,500 of these tests. What is the total cost per test?
items.why: Total cost per test is all costs for the period divided by the number of tests. **(₱45,000 + ₱30,000 + ₱15,000) ÷ 1,500 = ₱60 per test.** Leaving out labor or overhead underestimates the true cost and can lead to underpricing.

whyNot.0: This divides only the reagent and supply cost by the number of tests and leaves out labor and overhead.
whyNot.1: This includes reagents and labor but leaves out the allocated overhead.
whyNot.3: This adds reagents and overhead but leaves out labor.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Financial management: cost per test)

worked.problem: A laboratory spends ₱24,000 on reagents, ₱18,000 on labor, and ₱6,000 on overhead for a test in one month and performs 960 tests. What is the cost per test?
steps: Divide by the number of tests: ₱48,000 ÷ 960 = ₱50

items.stem: A newly organized laboratory makes sure that each medical technologist takes orders from, and reports to, only one immediate supervisor. Which principle of management is being applied?
items.why: **Unity of command means each employee receives orders from only one superior.** It prevents conflicting instructions and confusion about accountability.

whyNot.0: Span of control is the number of subordinates one supervisor can manage effectively, not how many bosses each worker has.
whyNot.1: Division of work is the specialization of tasks among staff, not the line of reporting.
whyNot.2: Centralization is about how much decision-making authority is kept at the top, not about single reporting lines.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Management principles; organizational structure)

items.stem: A medical technologist's salary, job security, and good relationships with coworkers are already satisfied. She is now most motivated by being recognized and respected for her expertise. In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, this corresponds to which level?
items.why: Maslow's hierarchy runs from physiological to safety, social, esteem, and self-actualization needs. **Recognition, respect, and status from others are esteem needs**, which become motivators once the lower levels are reasonably satisfied.

whyNot.0: Safety needs, such as job security and safe working conditions, are stated to be already met.
whyNot.2: Belonging needs, such as good relationships with coworkers, are stated to be already met.
whyNot.3: Self-actualization is fulfilling one's full potential through growth and creativity, which comes after recognition and respect.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Human resource management: motivation theories)

items.stem: A hospital posts an opening that requires a valid PRC license as a medical technologist and at least two years of histopathology experience. In job analysis, the statement of these minimum personal qualifications, kept separate from the list of the job's duties, is called the:
items.why: Job analysis yields two documents: the job description, which says what the job involves, and the job specification, which says **what qualifications a person needs to fill the job**, such as education, license, and experience.

whyNot.0: A job description lists the duties, responsibilities, and reporting relationships of the position rather than the qualifications of the person who fills it.
whyNot.1: A performance appraisal evaluates how well a current employee is doing the job; it is not used to define entry qualifications.
whyNot.3: An organizational chart shows positions and lines of authority, not the qualifications for a position.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Human resource management: job analysis)

items.stem: After reviewing the biopsy, the oncologist tells a patient that with treatment most people with this stage of disease are alive and well five years later. This forecast of the probable course and outcome of the disease is its:
items.why: The expected course and likely outcome of a disease, such as survival or chance of recovery, is its **prognosis**. It is based on factors like tumor grade, stage and response to treatment, and it is a prediction rather than a label for the disease itself.

whyNot.1: Diagnosis is the identification of what disease the patient has, not a forecast of how it will turn out.
whyNot.2: Pathogenesis is the sequence of cellular and molecular events by which the disease develops.
whyNot.3: Etiology is the cause of the disease, not its expected outcome.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Introduction to pathology)

items.stem: A breast mass feels stony hard and grates when cut. Microscopy shows small cords and nests of carcinoma cells scattered through abundant dense collagen. A tumor with this abundant fibrous stroma is described as:
items.why: Some carcinomas induce a heavy growth of collagen-rich stroma (desmoplasia), making the tumor rock-hard; such tumors are called **scirrhous**. The tumor cells (parenchyma) are relatively sparse compared with the fibrous stroma.

whyNot.0: A colloid (mucinous) carcinoma floats in pools of extracellular mucin and is soft and gelatinous, not stony hard.
whyNot.1: Papillary describes finger-like fronds of tumor cells on fibrovascular cores, not a dense fibrous stroma.
whyNot.3: A medullary tumor is the opposite: soft and fleshy, with sheets of tumor cells and very little stroma.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Neoplasia: nomenclature and characteristics)

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has progressive scarring of both lungs. Exposures, drugs, infections and autoimmune disease are all excluded after a full work-up, so the fibrosis is labeled as having no identifiable cause. Such a disease is described as:
items.why: A disease whose cause remains unknown after investigation is called **idiopathic**, as in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The term describes the gap in our knowledge of the etiology, not the severity of the disease.

whyNot.0: Iatrogenic means caused by medical treatment or a procedure, which was excluded here.
whyNot.1: Nosocomial means acquired in a hospital or health-care setting, usually an infection.
whyNot.2: Congenital means present at birth, which does not fit a disease that developed at age 60.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Introduction; Diseases of the lung)

items.stem: Type 2 diabetes mellitus clusters in families, yet it usually appears only when inherited susceptibility combines with obesity and physical inactivity. In terms of etiology, this disease is best classified as:
items.why: Disorders that arise from several susceptibility genes acting together with environmental influences are **multifactorial (complex) disorders**. Type 2 diabetes, hypertension and coronary artery disease are typical examples.

whyNot.0: Chromosomal disorders result from abnormal chromosome number or structure, such as trisomy 21.
whyNot.1: A single-gene (Mendelian) disorder follows a clear inheritance pattern from one mutant gene and does not need environmental triggers.
whyNot.2: A purely environmental cause would not explain the strong familial clustering of the disease.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Genetic and pediatric diseases; The endocrine system)

items.stem: After induction chemotherapy, a patient with acute leukemia has a normal blood count, no detectable blasts in the marrow, and no symptoms, although the physician does not yet consider her cured. This phase in the course of the disease is a:
items.why: A period in which the signs and symptoms of a disease abate or disappear, without proof of permanent cure, is a **remission**. If the disease later returns, that event is called a relapse.

whyNot.0: An exacerbation is a worsening or flare of signs and symptoms.
whyNot.1: A complication is a new, secondary problem arising from the disease or its treatment.
whyNot.3: A relapse is the return of the disease after a period of improvement, the opposite of what is described.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Introduction to pathology; Diseases of white blood cells)

items.stem: Celsus described four cardinal signs of acute inflammation: redness, heat, swelling and pain. Which fifth sign was later added by Rudolf Virchow?
items.why: The four classic signs listed by Celsus are rubor, calor, tumor and dolor. Virchow added a fifth, **loss of function (functio laesa)**, which results from pain, swelling and tissue damage at the inflamed site.

whyNot.0: Induration (firmness) can accompany chronic inflammation and fibrosis but is not one of the classic cardinal signs.
whyNot.1: Itching is a symptom of some allergic reactions but is not one of the cardinal signs of inflammation.
whyNot.2: Fever is a systemic acute-phase response, not a local cardinal sign of inflammation.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Inflammation and repair)

items.stem: At autopsy of a patient who died of acute pancreatitis, the peripancreatic fat contains scattered chalky-white, firm foci. Microscopy shows shadowy outlines of fat cells with basophilic calcium deposits. This pattern of cell death is:
items.why: Lipases released from the injured pancreas split triglycerides in adipocytes, and the freed fatty acids combine with calcium to form chalky-white soaps (saponification). This is **enzymatic fat necrosis**, the typical lesion of acute pancreatitis.

whyNot.0: Caseous necrosis is the cheesy, friable necrosis seen in granulomas such as tuberculosis.
whyNot.1: Gangrenous necrosis refers to ischemic necrosis of a limb or bowel, often with superimposed bacterial infection.
whyNot.2: Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture in solid organs after ischemia, such as myocardial or renal infarcts, and is not linked to saponification.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Cell injury, cell death and adaptations)

items.stem: A skin biopsy shows occasional single keratinocytes that are shrunken, with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and condensed, fragmented nuclei. Neighboring cells are intact and there is no surrounding inflammation. These findings best indicate:
items.why: Death of isolated single cells with cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation and fragmentation, and no inflammatory reaction is characteristic of **apoptosis**. The plasma membrane stays intact and the fragments are removed by phagocytes before cell contents leak out, so inflammation is not triggered.

whyNot.0: Coagulative necrosis usually affects groups of cells in an area, with cell swelling, membrane damage and an inflammatory reaction.
whyNot.2: Liquefactive necrosis digests tissue into a fluid mass, typically in abscesses or brain infarcts, with abundant inflammation.
whyNot.3: Hydropic swelling is a reversible change in which cells enlarge and become pale, not shrunken and dense.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Cell injury, cell death and adaptations)

items.stem: A whole brain removed at autopsy is to be fixed intact in 10% formalin for later cutting. How should it be placed in the fixative to prevent distortion of its shape?
options: Pack the container tightly with dry cotton around the brain
Cut it into 1 cm coronal slabs before placing it in fixative
Lay it flat on the bottom of the container, base downward
Suspend it upside down by a string passed under the basilar artery
items.why: A fresh brain is very soft and will flatten under its own weight if it rests on the container floor. It is therefore **suspended in a large volume of formalin by a thread passed beneath the basilar artery**, so it floats free while it hardens over about two weeks.

whyNot.0: Dry cotton does not support the brain evenly and would leave parts of it out of contact with fixative.
whyNot.1: Fresh brain is too soft to slice cleanly; it is normally fixed whole and cut only after it has hardened.
whyNot.2: Resting the soft fresh brain on the container floor flattens and distorts it.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Fixation of special specimens)

items.stem: A testicular biopsy fixed in Bouin's fluid is bright yellow. What is the recommended way to remove the excess picric acid after fixation?
options: Wash it in running tap water overnight
items.why: Picric acid is removed with alcohol, so Bouin's-fixed tissue is taken **directly into 50–70% ethanol**, which is also the first dehydration step. Washing in water is avoided because the picrate–protein complexes are water-soluble and can be lost.

whyNot.1: Sodium thiosulfate removes the iodine color after mercury pigment removal; it has no role with picric acid.
whyNot.2: Alcoholic iodine is used to remove mercuric chloride pigment, not picric acid.
whyNot.3: Water washing is the step to avoid after Bouin's, because the picrate–protein complexes are water-soluble.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: picric acid fixatives); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Fixation)

items.stem: A hematopathology service asks for a fixative containing mercuric chloride and sodium acetate, with formaldehyde added just before use. It is chosen for crisp nuclear detail in bone marrow and lymph node biopsies. Which fixative is this?
items.why: **B-5** is a mercuric chloride–sodium acetate stock to which formaldehyde is added at the time of use. It gives sharp nuclear chromatin detail valued in lymphoma and marrow diagnosis, but it leaves mercury pigment and requires hazardous-waste disposal.

whyNot.0: Bouin's fluid is a picric acid–formaldehyde–acetic acid mixture and contains no mercury.
whyNot.1: Carnoy's fluid is a mixture of ethanol, chloroform and glacial acetic acid.
whyNot.2: Orth's fluid is a potassium dichromate–formaldehyde (chromate) fixative.

items.ref: Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Fixation); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation)

items.stem: Which fixative both preserves lipids and stains them black, and is also used as a secondary fixative for electron microscopy specimens?
items.why: **Osmium tetroxide** reacts with unsaturated lipids, fixing them and being reduced to a black deposit. In electron microscopy it is used after glutaraldehyde to fix membranes and add electron density.

whyNot.1: Mercuric chloride is a protein-coagulating fixative that leaves black mercury pigment, not stained lipids.
whyNot.2: Potassium dichromate preserves some lipids and mitochondria but does not stain lipids black.
whyNot.3: Glutaraldehyde is the primary aldehyde fixative for electron microscopy but does not fix or blacken lipids.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: osmium tetroxide); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Fixation)

items.stem: An intact, unopened spleen weighing 400 g was placed in a generous volume of 10% formalin. Sections taken two days later show good fixation at the surface but autolysis in the center. What should have been done when the specimen was received?
options: Fix it whole in formalin heated to 60 °C
Slice it at about 1 cm intervals before immersion
Store it whole at 4 °C in the same formalin
items.why: Formaldehyde penetrates tissue slowly, about a millimeter per hour, so the center of a large solid organ autolyzes before fixative reaches it. Large organs should be **sliced into thin slabs (bread-loafed) so that fixative reaches all surfaces quickly**.

whyNot.0: Heating a whole organ overfixes and cooks the outside before the center is reached.
whyNot.1: Doubling the formalin strength does not overcome slow penetration and increases hardening at the surface.
whyNot.3: Cold slows autolysis but also slows penetration and fixation; it does not solve the problem of thickness.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: factors affecting fixation)

items.stem: A fresh muscle sample is to be fixed for demonstration of phosphatase and lipase activity, which diffuse easily and are destroyed by most fixatives. Which fixative is classically used for such enzyme studies?
items.why: **Cold acetone** fixes rapidly by dehydration while preserving much enzyme activity, so it is the classic fixative for water-diffusible enzymes such as phosphatases and lipases. Many enzyme methods use unfixed cryostat sections or only brief cold fixation for the same reason.

whyNot.1: Bouin's fluid is strongly acidic because of picric and acetic acids and destroys enzyme activity.
whyNot.2: Heat denatures enzymes; hot formalin would inactivate the very activity to be demonstrated.
whyNot.3: Zenker's fluid contains mercuric chloride and acetic acid, which inactivate most enzymes.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Fixation: acetone); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Enzyme histochemistry)

items.stem: Sections of a hemorrhagic tumor contain brown-black birefringent deposits identified as formalin pigment. Which treatment of the sections before staining will remove this pigment?
options: Alcoholic iodine followed by sodium thiosulfate
Potassium permanganate followed by oxalic acid
items.why: Acid formaldehyde hematin forms when acidic formalin reacts with hemoglobin. It dissolves in alkaline alcohol, so it is removed with **ammonia in alcohol (Kardasewitsch method)** or with alcoholic picric acid.

whyNot.1: Iodine followed by thiosulfate removes mercuric chloride pigment and does not dissolve formalin pigment.
whyNot.2: Permanganate followed by oxalic acid is an oxidative bleaching method for melanin, not for formalin pigment.
whyNot.3: Warm water does not dissolve formalin pigment and may loosen sections from the slide.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: artifacts and pigments); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Pigments and minerals)

items.stem: Which fixative acts by removing water from proteins so that they coagulate, without becoming chemically bound to the tissue?
items.why: Alcohols such as **ethanol** fix by dehydrating and coagulating proteins; they are coagulant, non-additive fixatives because they are not incorporated into the tissue. They preserve some antigens and nucleic acids well but cause shrinkage and hardening.

whyNot.1: Glutaraldehyde is also an additive cross-linking aldehyde, with two aldehyde groups per molecule.
whyNot.2: Mercuric chloride is additive: it combines with protein groups and leaves mercury in the tissue.
whyNot.3: Formaldehyde is additive: it binds to proteins and cross-links them with methylene bridges.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: mechanisms of fixation)

items.stem: A 2 mm endoscopic gastric biopsy was left on a dry gauze pad on the bench for 40 minutes before it was put into formalin. Which handling would have best protected it from artifact?
options: Wrapping it in dry tissue paper to keep it flat
Placing it in formalin immediately after removal
Placing it in a −20 °C freezer until it is collected
Holding it in normal saline overnight before fixing
items.why: Tiny biopsies dry out within minutes, causing shrinkage and distortion, and autolysis starts as soon as tissue loses its blood supply. The specimen should be **put into an adequate volume of fixative immediately after removal**.

whyNot.0: Dry paper draws fluid out of the biopsy and makes the drying artifact worse.
whyNot.2: Slow freezing forms ice crystals that disrupt the tissue structure.
whyNot.3: Prolonged storage in saline allows autolysis and swelling before fixation.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: practical aspects); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Handling of specimens)

items.stem: A study of mitochondria uses Regaud's fluid, a potassium dichromate–formalin fixative. Before the tissue is dehydrated, it must be handled correctly to keep an insoluble dark deposit from forming in it. What should be done?
options: Wash it thoroughly in running water
Treat it with iodine, then sodium thiosulfate
Rinse it briefly in alcoholic ammonia
items.why: If dichromate-fixed tissue goes straight into alcohol, chromium compounds precipitate as a dark, insoluble chrome pigment. The tissue is therefore **washed well in running water, preferably for several hours or overnight, before dehydration**.

whyNot.0: Going straight into alcohol is what causes the chrome precipitate; direct transfer to 70% ethanol is the rule for Bouin's-fixed tissue, not dichromate-fixed tissue.
whyNot.2: Iodine followed by sodium thiosulfate removes mercury pigment left by mercuric chloride fixatives.
whyNot.3: Alcoholic ammonia removes formalin (acid formaldehyde hematin) pigment from sections; it is not the step after dichromate fixation.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fixation: dichromate fixatives); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Fixation: chromate fixatives)

items.stem: A small bone biopsy must be decalcified without spoiling nuclear staining or later immunohistochemistry. Which acid is slower than the strong mineral acids but gentle enough to be the usual choice for such specimens?
items.why: **Formic acid** is a weak organic acid that decalcifies more slowly than nitric or hydrochloric acid but causes much less damage to nuclear staining and antigens. It is often used with formalin or a buffer and suits most routine surgical bone specimens.

whyNot.0: Hydrochloric acid is also a strong mineral acid that works fast but harms nuclear staining.
whyNot.2: Nitric acid is a strong, rapid decalcifier that easily damages staining and antigens if exposure is prolonged.
whyNot.3: Sulfuric acid is unsuitable because it forms insoluble calcium sulfate that stays in the tissue.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Bone: decalcification); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Decalcification)

items.stem: A femoral head was placed in 10% nitric acid, and the decalcification endpoint was not checked until a week later. In the H&E sections, the nuclei are pale and stain poorly with hematoxylin, while the eosin is bright. What is the most likely cause?
options: Sections cut too thin on the microtome
items.why: Strong acid hydrolyzes nucleic acids, so **over-decalcification** leaves nuclei that take up hematoxylin weakly while eosin staining is preserved or enhanced. This is why the endpoint must be checked and the tissue removed and rinsed as soon as decalcification is complete.

whyNot.0: Thin sections stain somewhat lighter overall, but would not selectively spare eosin.
whyNot.1: Incomplete dehydration causes milky clearing and poor wax infiltration, not selective loss of nuclear staining.
whyNot.3: Formalin pigment appears as brown-black granules, not as pale, weakly stained nuclei.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Bone: decalcification); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Decalcification)

items.stem: In electrolytic decalcification, a current is passed through an acid solution containing the bone. Toward which electrode do the released calcium ions move?
options: Toward neither electrode, staying bound in the bone
items.why: Calcium ions carry a positive charge (Ca²⁺), so in an electric field they migrate **toward the cathode, the negative electrode**. Removing them from around the bone speeds decalcification, although the heat produced can damage tissue.

whyNot.0: The anode is positive and repels the positively charged calcium ions.
whyNot.1: Charged ions move toward the electrode of opposite charge, not equally to both.
whyNot.2: The acid releases calcium from the bone mineral; once released, the ions are free to move in the field.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Decalcification); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Bone)

items.stem: A small, delicate embryo is to be processed into paraffin. How should dehydration be started compared with routine adult surgical tissue?
options: Begin in xylene before any alcohol
Begin in a lower-grade alcohol, about 30%
items.why: Abrupt transfer from an aqueous fixative into strong alcohol creates strong diffusion currents that shrink and distort fragile tissue. Delicate specimens such as embryos are therefore **started in a low grade of alcohol (around 30%)** and moved through gradual steps.

whyNot.0: Strong, heated alcohol makes the shrinkage and hardening even worse.
whyNot.1: Xylene is not miscible with water, so it cannot be used before the tissue is dehydrated.
whyNot.2: Going straight into absolute alcohol causes severe shrinkage and distortion of delicate tissue.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: dehydration); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Dehydration)

items.stem: A layer of anhydrous copper sulfate is kept under a filter paper at the bottom of the last absolute alcohol bath. If this white powder turns blue, what should the technologist do?
options: Nothing, as blue shows the alcohol is fully anhydrous
Replace the alcohol, which has taken up water
Shorten the clearing step that follows
Add xylene to the bath to remove the color
items.why: Anhydrous copper sulfate is white and turns blue when it absorbs water. A blue color means the **'absolute' alcohol is contaminated with water and should be changed**, otherwise dehydration will be incomplete.

whyNot.0: Blue is the hydrated form of copper sulfate, which shows that water is present, not that the alcohol is dry.
whyNot.2: Shortening clearing does not correct water left in the tissue and would cause further problems.
whyNot.3: Xylene would not remove water and is not miscible with water, so it would make clearing worse.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Dehydration); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing)

items.stem: With most clearing agents, the endpoint of clearing is judged by the tissue becoming translucent. Which clearing agent does NOT make tissue translucent, so its endpoint cannot be judged this way?
items.why: **Chloroform** removes alcohol and is miscible with paraffin, but it does not raise the refractive index of tissue enough to make it look clear. Clearing time must therefore be based on block size and experience rather than on appearance.

whyNot.1: Toluene behaves much like xylene and also renders tissue translucent.
whyNot.2: Xylene makes tissue translucent quickly, so clearing is easy to judge visually.
whyNot.3: Cedarwood oil is slow but makes tissue very clear, and is used for delicate specimens such as the central nervous system.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Clearing); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: clearing)

items.stem: Because of a long holiday weekend, a batch of tissues stayed in xylene for three days during processing. What is the most likely effect on the tissues?
options: They lose all affinity for eosin when stained
They remain soft, as if they had never been fixed
They become hard and brittle and crumble when cut
They become milky and opaque in the paraffin
items.why: Xylene clears quickly, and prolonged exposure **over-hardens tissue, making it brittle so that sections crumble or crack**. Clearing times are therefore kept short and matched to block size.

whyNot.0: Prolonged xylene does not specifically remove eosin staining.
whyNot.1: Soft, mushy tissue suggests incomplete fixation, the opposite of overhardening.
whyNot.3: A milky, opaque appearance in xylene points to water left from incomplete dehydration, not overlong clearing.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: clearing); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Clearing)

items.stem: Lung and other spongy tissues are often infiltrated with paraffin under reduced pressure in a vacuum infiltrator. What is the main purpose of the vacuum?
options: To lower the melting point of the paraffin wax
To harden the tissue further before embedding
To remove remaining water left after dehydration
To remove trapped air so wax penetrates faster
items.why: Reduced pressure pulls air bubbles and volatile clearing agent out of the tissue spaces, so **molten wax replaces them more quickly and completely**. This shortens infiltration time and gives better blocks of lung, bone and dense tissue.

whyNot.0: Vacuum has no meaningful effect on the melting point of paraffin wax.
whyNot.1: The vacuum does not harden tissue; hardening comes from fixation and processing reagents.
whyNot.2: Water should already be removed during dehydration; vacuum infiltration cannot correct poor dehydration.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: infiltration); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Processing)

items.stem: Fixed tissue is taken straight from aqueous solution into a molten wax-like medium, skipping dehydration and clearing, so that lipids and some enzymes are not extracted by solvents. Which embedding medium is used this way?
items.why: **Polyethylene glycol (Carbowax)** is water-soluble, so tissue can go into it without dehydration or clearing, preserving lipids and some enzymes. A drawback is that the sections dissolve or distort when floated on plain water.

whyNot.0: Celloidin is dissolved in ether–alcohol, so the tissue must first be dehydrated.
whyNot.1: Paraffin is not miscible with water, so tissue must be dehydrated and cleared first, which extracts lipids.
whyNot.3: Epoxy resins need the tissue dehydrated, usually through ethanol and often propylene oxide, before infiltration.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: embedding media); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Infiltration and embedding)

items.stem: For electron microscopy, tissue embedded in epoxy resin is first cut into 0.5–1 µm 'semithin' sections to choose the area for ultrathin sectioning. Which stain is routinely applied to these semithin sections?
items.why: Semithin resin sections are stained with **toluidine blue**, often on a hot plate, which penetrates resin and gives a quick view of the tissue under the light microscope. The block is then trimmed to the chosen area for ultrathin sections.

whyNot.1: Routine H&E stains resin-embedded tissue poorly because the resin is not removed from the section.
whyNot.2: Uranyl acetate is a heavy-metal contrast stain for ultrathin sections on EM grids, not a light microscopy stain.
whyNot.3: Oil red O is a fat stain for frozen sections, not for resin-embedded tissue.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Electron microscopy; Plastic embedding)

items.stem: During trimming, a paraffin block smells strongly of xylene and the tissue is soft and crumbles out of the wax. What is the most likely cause?
options: A dull edge on the microtome knife
Overfixation of the tissue in formalin
items.why: A smell of clearing agent in the block means that **xylene was not fully replaced by wax during infiltration**, often because the wax was contaminated or infiltration was too short. The tissue should be returned to fresh molten wax and re-embedded.

whyNot.1: A dull knife produces sectioning faults; it does not cause the block to smell of clearing agent.
whyNot.2: Overfixation makes tissue hard and brittle, not soft and smelling of xylene.
whyNot.3: Over-decalcification damages staining and may soften bone, but does not leave xylene in the block.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Tissue processing: troubleshooting); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Faults in processing)

items.stem: On a warm afternoon, paraffin sections come off the microtome compressed and wrinkled, and wax builds up on the knife edge. Which corrective step should be tried first?
options: Chill the block on ice and use a sharp blade area
Switch to egg albumin as the adhesive
Raise the flotation bath to about 65 °C
Warm the block in the oven before cutting
items.why: Compression and wrinkling come mainly from a block that is too soft or warm and from a dull or wax-coated edge. **Cooling the block face on ice and using a clean, sharp part of the blade** usually corrects the fault.

whyNot.1: The adhesive acts only after flotation and has no effect on compression during cutting.
whyNot.2: A very hot bath melts the wax and makes the sections fall apart; it does not prevent compression at the knife.
whyNot.3: Warming makes the wax softer and increases compression.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: troubleshooting); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Microtomy)

items.stem: A ribbon of paraffin sections comes off the microtome curved to one side instead of straight. What is the most likely cause?
options: A flotation bath that is too warm
Upper and lower block edges not parallel
Static electricity in very dry air
items.why: When the top and bottom edges of the block face are not parallel to each other and to the knife edge, one side of each section is longer than the other, so **the ribbon curves**. Re-trimming the block so these edges are parallel corrects it.

whyNot.0: The flotation bath is used after cutting and cannot change the shape of the ribbon at the knife.
whyNot.1: Over-decalcification affects staining quality, not the shape of the ribbon.
whyNot.3: Static makes sections cling to the knife or fly about, but does not cause a curved ribbon.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: troubleshooting); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Sectioning faults)

items.stem: A block of hard, densely fibrous tissue yields sections with regular bands of alternating thick and thin zones running parallel to the knife edge, like a venetian blind. The knife and block holder are tight. What is the most likely cause?
options: A nick in the cutting edge of the knife
Knife vibration against the hard tissue
Static electricity in the cutting area
items.why: Bands parallel to the knife edge within each section are **chatter, caused by the knife vibrating as it meets very hard tissue** (or a block that is not held rigidly). Softening the block face, cutting more slowly and checking the knife tilt help.

whyNot.0: A nick produces a score line running perpendicular to the knife edge, at the same place in every section.
whyNot.2: Static makes sections cling or curl, but does not cause bands of varying thickness.
whyNot.3: Incomplete dehydration causes poor infiltration and crumbling, not regular bands.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: troubleshooting); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Microtomy)

items.stem: In a cold, air-conditioned room, a technologist cuts a block embedded in a high-melting-point paraffin. The block edges are parallel and the knife is sharp, but the sections come off one at a time and will not join into a ribbon. Which remedy is most likely to help?
options: Chill the block face on ice before each cut
Coat the block's top and bottom edges with softer wax
Increase the knife tilt to a steeper angle
Cut thicker sections, at about 15–20 µm
items.why: Sections join into a ribbon because the wax at their edges is just soft enough to stick together. When the wax is too hard for the room temperature, they separate, so **coating the upper and lower edges of the block with a softer, lower-melting-point wax (or re-embedding in softer wax)** restores ribboning.

whyNot.0: Chilling makes the wax harder still, which is the opposite of what an over-hard block needs.
whyNot.2: Excessive knife tilt is itself a cause of failure to form a ribbon, so increasing it would make the fault worse.
whyNot.3: Sections that are too thick also fail to ribbon, and routine paraffin sections are cut at only about 3–5 µm.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Sectioning: faults and remedies); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy: troubleshooting)

items.stem: Of the three traditional steel microtome knife profiles, one has a plain triangular cross-section with neither side hollow-ground, which gives it the most rigid edge. Which profile is this, and for what work is it traditionally recommended?
options: Plane-wedge; frozen sections and very hard tissue in paraffin
Biconcave; frozen sections and very hard tissue in paraffin
Plano-concave; celloidin blocks on a sliding microtome
Plane-wedge; celloidin blocks on a sliding microtome
items.why: A **plane-wedge knife** has two flat sides meeting at the edge, so the edge is thick and rigid. It is traditionally recommended for frozen sections and for tough or hard tissue embedded in paraffin.

whyNot.1: A biconcave knife has both sides hollow-ground, giving a thinner, less rigid edge suited to routine paraffin sections, not frozen or very hard tissue.
whyNot.2: A plano-concave knife does suit celloidin on a sliding microtome, but it has one flat and one concave side, not a plain triangular profile.
whyNot.3: The profile is named correctly, but celloidin sectioning is traditionally done with a plano-concave knife, not a plane-wedge knife.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Microtome knives); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microtomy)

items.stem: Paraffin sections keep floating off their slides during heat-induced antigen retrieval for immunohistochemistry. What change is most likely to prevent this?
options: Dry the slides at room temperature only
Cut thicker sections of about 10 µm
Use positively charged or silane-coated slides
Float sections on a cooler water bath
items.why: Heating in retrieval buffer loosens sections from plain glass. **Positively charged, poly-L-lysine or silane (APES)-coated slides** bind the negatively charged tissue firmly so sections survive retrieval and long staining runs.

whyNot.0: Thorough drying, often at about 60 °C, improves adhesion; drying only at room temperature makes lifting more likely.
whyNot.1: Thicker sections are heavier and more likely to lift, and they spoil IHC interpretation.
whyNot.3: Bath temperature affects flattening, not how strongly the section adheres during retrieval.

items.ref: Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Immunohistochemistry); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Immunohistochemical techniques)

items.stem: For an intraoperative frozen section, the fresh tissue is surrounded by a water-soluble mixture of glycols and resins and frozen onto the cryostat chuck. What is this medium?
items.why: **OCT compound** is a water-soluble glycol–resin medium that freezes around fresh tissue, holding it on the chuck and supporting it during cryostat sectioning. It washes off the section in aqueous solutions during staining.

whyNot.0: Celloidin is a slow nitrocellulose embedding medium for large or hard tissue, not for frozen sections.
whyNot.2: Paraffin requires fixed, dehydrated and cleared tissue and is not used for fresh frozen sections.
whyNot.3: Canada balsam is a resinous mounting medium used under the coverslip, not an embedding medium.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Frozen sections); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Frozen sections)

items.stem: Cryostat sections keep curling up and rolling onto the knife as they are cut. Which part of the cryostat is adjusted to keep each section flat on the knife?
items.why: The **anti-roll plate** is a glass or plastic guide set just above and parallel to the knife edge, so each section slides flat beneath it instead of curling. Its height and angle must be adjusted carefully, or a fine brush can be used instead.

whyNot.1: The defrost timer controls periodic defrosting of the chamber and has nothing to do with rolling sections.
whyNot.2: Changing thickness alters the section but is not the device that keeps it flat.
whyNot.3: Temperature affects how well tissue cuts but does not by itself stop a section from rolling.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Frozen sections: the cryostat)

items.stem: How many mL of concentrated (70%) nitric acid are needed to prepare 250 mL of a 5% nitric acid decalcifying solution? (Treat both percentages as v/v.)
items.why: Use C1V1 = C2V2: (70%)(V1) = (5%)(250 mL), so V1 = 1,250 / 70 = **about 17.9 mL of 70% nitric acid**, made up to 250 mL with water. Acid is always added to the water, never the reverse.

whyNot.0: 25 mL of 70% acid in 250 mL is a 1-in-10 dilution, which gives 7% acid, not 5%.
whyNot.1: About 232.1 mL is the volume of water to add (250 − 17.9), not the volume of acid.
whyNot.2: 12.5 mL is 5% of 250 mL; this assumes the stock is 100% acid and ignores its 70% strength.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Bone: decalcification); Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Laboratory solutions)

worked.problem: How many mL of 90% formic acid are needed to make 500 mL of 10% formic acid?
steps: Add the acid to about 444 mL of water to make a final volume of 500 mL.
worked.result: About 55.6 mL of 90% formic acid, diluted to 500 mL

items.stem: Encapsulated yeasts are seen in a lung biopsy. Which stain colors the mucopolysaccharide capsule red, helping to identify Cryptococcus neoformans among yeasts of similar size?
items.why: **Mucicarmine** stains epithelial mucin and the mucopolysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus red. Most other yeasts of similar size do not have a mucicarmine-positive capsule, so the stain helps confirm the organism.

whyNot.1: GMS stains the cell walls of almost all fungi black, so it shows yeasts but does not single out Cryptococcus by its capsule.
whyNot.2: Perls' Prussian blue demonstrates ferric iron (hemosiderin), not fungi.
whyNot.3: Ziehl–Neelsen stains acid-fast bacilli such as mycobacteria, not fungal capsules.

items.ref: Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Microorganisms); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microorganisms)

items.stem: Two serial sections of a mucin-rich tumor are stained with Alcian blue, one at pH 2.5 and one at pH 1.0. Mucin that stains blue at pH 1.0 is mainly of which type?
options: Mucins rich in carboxyl (sialic acid) groups
items.why: At pH 2.5, Alcian blue binds both carboxylated and sulfated acid mucins. At pH 1.0 the carboxyl groups are no longer ionized, so **only the strongly acidic sulfated mucins** still stain.

whyNot.0: Glycogen is not an acidic mucosubstance and is demonstrated with PAS and diastase, not Alcian blue.
whyNot.1: Neutral mucins carry no acidic groups and do not stain with Alcian blue at either pH; they are PAS-positive.
whyNot.3: Carboxylated (sialylated) mucins stain at pH 2.5 but lose their charge and stop staining at pH 1.0.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Carbohydrates); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Carbohydrates)

items.stem: In a liver biopsy, the pathologist wants to see whether the fine framework of fibers supporting the hepatocyte plates has collapsed. Which stain is best, and how do these fibers appear?
items.why: Reticulin (type III collagen) fibers are argyrophilic and are shown by **silver impregnation methods such as Gordon and Sweets, which stain them black**. Collapse or loss of this framework is important in assessing liver necrosis and tumors.

whyNot.0: Masson's trichrome stains collagen blue or green and muscle and cytoplasm red; it is not the method for fine reticulin.
whyNot.1: Perls' method shows ferric iron, not connective tissue fibers.
whyNot.2: Congo red demonstrates amyloid, with apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Connective tissues and mesenchymal tissues); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Connective tissue)

items.stem: A temporal artery biopsy is examined for fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina. Which stain is commonly used, and what color are the elastic fibers?
items.why: **Verhoeff's iron hematoxylin stains elastic fibers black**, and the Van Gieson counterstain colors collagen red and muscle yellow. This makes breaks in the internal elastic lamina easy to see.

whyNot.0: Van Gieson alone stains collagen red and muscle yellow but does not demonstrate elastic fibers.
whyNot.2: Perls' method stains ferric iron and does not show elastic tissue.
whyNot.3: Oil red O is a frozen-section fat stain and does not show elastic fibers.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Connective tissues); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Connective tissue)

items.stem: When Harris hematoxylin is prepared, mercuric oxide is added to the hot dye solution. What is the purpose of this ingredient?
options: It oxidizes hematoxylin to hematein, the colored dye
It is the mordant that links the dye to chromatin
It acidifies the solution to sharpen nuclear staining
It stops mold from growing during storage
items.why: Hematoxylin itself is nearly colorless and must be oxidized ('ripened') to **hematein**, the active coloring agent. Harris's formula ripens it chemically with mercuric oxide (many current formulas use sodium iodate instead), so the stain is ready almost at once instead of after weeks of natural oxidation.

whyNot.1: The mordant in Harris hematoxylin is the aluminum salt (potassium or ammonium alum), which binds hematein to nuclear chromatin.
whyNot.2: Acidity comes from glacial acetic acid, which many laboratories add to make nuclear staining more selective.
whyNot.3: Preservatives such as chloral hydrate or thymol, not mercuric oxide, are used in some hematoxylin formulas to prevent mold.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Hematoxylin and eosin); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Nuclear and cytoplasmic staining)

items.stem: A light nuclear counterstain is needed after immunohistochemistry, applied until the right intensity is reached and with no differentiation step. Which hematoxylin is most commonly used in this progressive way?
items.why: **Mayer's hematoxylin** is a dilute alum hematoxylin that is commonly used progressively, so nuclei are stained to the desired depth without acid differentiation. This makes it a common counterstain for IHC, where acid could harm the chromogen or the section.

whyNot.0: PTAH is a tungsten hematoxylin used for fibrin and muscle cross-striations, not as a routine counterstain.
whyNot.1: Heidenhain's iron hematoxylin is a regressive stain that is differentiated in iron alum, used for detail such as muscle striations.
whyNot.3: Weigert's iron hematoxylin resists acid and is used before picric acid–containing counterstains such as Van Gieson.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Hematoxylin and eosin); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Nuclear and cytoplasmic staining)

items.stem: A section stained with toluidine blue shows blue nuclei, while the granules of mast cells are reddish-purple. Staining tissue a color different from that of the dye solution is called:
items.why: When a dye stains certain tissue components a color different from the dye itself, the reaction is **metachromasia**. Highly sulfated substances such as mast cell heparin stack the dye molecules and shift their color from blue to red-purple.

whyNot.1: Birefringence is double refraction seen under polarized light, not a staining color change.
whyNot.2: Argyrophilia is the ability to bind silver, which then requires a reducer to be seen.
whyNot.3: Orthochromasia is staining in the same color as the dye, as seen in the blue nuclei here.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Theory of staining); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Dyes and staining)

items.stem: A skin biopsy from a patient with suspected leprosy is negative with the routine Ziehl–Neelsen stain. A modified acid-fast method uses an oil–xylene mixture to remove paraffin and a weaker acid decolorizer, and red bacilli are then seen. Which method is this?
items.why: Mycobacterium leprae is less acid-fast than M. tuberculosis and loses carbol fuchsin after harsh solvents and strong acid. The **Fite–Faraco (Wade–Fite) method** protects the bacterial lipid wall with oil during dewaxing and uses gentler decolorization, so the bacilli stay red.

whyNot.0: GMS is a silver method used mainly for fungi and Pneumocystis, not for acid-fast staining.
whyNot.1: Auramine–rhodamine is a fluorescent method in which mycobacteria glow yellow-orange under UV, not red under bright-field.
whyNot.3: Brown–Brenn is a tissue Gram stain that separates gram-positive from gram-negative bacteria.

items.ref: Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Microorganisms); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Microorganisms)

items.stem: A liver mass in a patient with no known primary is a metastatic adenocarcinoma. Immunohistochemistry shows CK7 negative, CK20 positive and CDX2 positive. Which primary site is most likely?
items.why: The pattern **CK7-negative, CK20-positive, with nuclear CDX2, is typical of colorectal adenocarcinoma**. Most carcinomas of the lung, breast and ovary show the reverse pattern, CK7-positive and CK20-negative.

whyNot.0: Ovarian serous carcinoma is typically CK7-positive, CK20-negative and WT1-positive.
whyNot.1: Lung adenocarcinoma is usually CK7-positive, CK20-negative and often TTF-1-positive.
whyNot.2: Breast carcinoma is usually CK7-positive and CK20-negative, often with GATA3 positivity.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Neoplasia: diagnosis); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Immunohistochemistry in diagnosis)

items.stem: An immunoperoxidase stain detected with DAB shows brown red cells and neutrophils in every section, including the negative control from which the primary antibody was left out. Which step was most likely omitted?
options: Blocking endogenous alkaline phosphatase with levamisole
Blocking endogenous peroxidase with hydrogen peroxide
items.why: Red cells (pseudoperoxidase of hemoglobin) and granulocytes contain enzymes that convert DAB to a brown product on their own. **Treating sections with hydrogen peroxide (for example in methanol) blocks this endogenous peroxidase** before the antibodies are applied.

whyNot.0: Leaving out the counterstain would remove the blue nuclei, not cause brown staining of blood cells.
whyNot.1: Levamisole blocks endogenous alkaline phosphatase, which matters only for AP-based detection, not HRP–DAB.
whyNot.3: Omitting antigen retrieval weakens true staining; it does not cause brown staining in the no-primary control.

items.ref: Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Immunohistochemical techniques); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Immunohistochemistry)

items.stem: Cervical smears from a rural clinic were fixed with an alcohol spray fixative containing polyethylene glycol (Carbowax). What must be done in the laboratory before Papanicolaou staining?
options: Heat-fix the slides by passing them through a flame
Soak the slides in 95% alcohol to dissolve the wax coat
Let the slides air-dry and stain them with Giemsa
Rinse the slides in xylene to remove the wax coat
items.why: The polyethylene glycol in spray fixatives leaves a protective film on the smear that blocks uptake of the stains. The **slides are soaked in 95% alcohol (or rinsed in water) for several minutes to remove the coating** before they enter the Pap staining series.

whyNot.0: Flame heat-fixing is used for bacteriologic smears and would destroy cell detail in a cytology smear.
whyNot.2: The smears are already alcohol-fixed for Pap staining; air-drying and Giemsa staining would change the method.
whyNot.3: Xylene is the clearing agent used at the end of the Pap sequence; the standard way to remove the coating is a soak in alcohol before staining begins.

items.ref: Koss' Diagnostic Cytology and Its Histopathologic Bases, 5th ed. (Laboratory techniques); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Cytology)

items.stem: A large, protein-rich pleural effusion is to be sent for cytology, and fluids from this patient have formed fibrin clots before. What can be added at collection to prevent clotting?
items.why: Fibrin clots trap cells and make smears and cytospins poor. A small amount of **heparin added to the collection container** prevents clotting without harming the cells.

whyNot.1: Formalin fixation hardens the cells and gives poor results with the Papanicolaou stain.
whyNot.2: Saline dilutes the specimen but does not stop the fibrin from clotting.
whyNot.3: Adding strong alcohol to a protein-rich fluid coagulates the protein into a dense clot that traps cells.

items.ref: Koss' Diagnostic Cytology and Its Histopathologic Bases, 5th ed. (Effusions; Laboratory techniques)

items.stem: Under The Bethesda System, what is the minimum number of well-preserved endocervical or squamous metaplastic cells needed to report that a transformation zone component is present?
items.why: The Bethesda System notes a transformation zone component as present when **at least 10 well-preserved endocervical or squamous metaplastic cells** are seen, singly or in clusters. Its absence is reported as a quality indicator but does not by itself make the specimen unsatisfactory.

whyNot.0: Fifty cells is far above the Bethesda requirement for this component.
whyNot.1: Five cells is below the number Bethesda requires to report the transformation zone component as present.
whyNot.2: One hundred cells is not the Bethesda threshold for the transformation zone component.

items.ref: The Bethesda System for Reporting Cervical Cytology, 3rd ed. (2014 terminology) (Specimen adequacy)

items.stem: A cervical smear shows mature squamous cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic, wrinkled nuclei, some binucleate, each surrounded by a sharply outlined clear perinuclear cavity. Under The Bethesda System, this is reported as:
items.why: These are koilocytes, the cytopathic effect of HPV in mature squamous cells. Bethesda reports them as **LSIL**, which also includes mild dysplasia (CIN 1).

whyNot.0: NILM would ignore a definite viral cytopathic change that qualifies as an intraepithelial lesion.
whyNot.2: HSIL involves immature cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, not mature koilocytes.
whyNot.3: ASC-US is used when changes are suggestive but not enough for SIL; well-formed koilocytes are definite LSIL.

items.ref: The Bethesda System for Reporting Cervical Cytology, 3rd ed. (2014 terminology) (Squamous cell abnormalities); Koss' Diagnostic Cytology and Its Histopathologic Bases, 5th ed. (Cervix)

items.stem: A Pap smear from a 72-year-old woman on no hormone therapy consists almost entirely of small, round squamous cells with relatively large nuclei, and very few superficial cells. What does this maturation pattern indicate?
items.why: Without estrogen, the squamous epithelium does not mature, so parabasal cells predominate, a 'shift to the left' in the maturation index. This **atrophic pattern** is expected after menopause without hormone replacement.

whyNot.0: Strong estrogen effect produces mostly mature superficial cells, the opposite pattern.
whyNot.1: Progesterone effect gives mostly intermediate cells, often folded and clustered (navicular cells).
whyNot.3: Inflammation does not by itself cause a parabasal-predominant maturation pattern.

items.ref: Koss' Diagnostic Cytology and Its Histopathologic Bases, 5th ed. (Normal female genital tract; hormonal cytology)

items.stem: A thick, viscous sputum sample is to be spread for cytology. A small portion is placed between two slides, pressed gently, and the slides are drawn apart. What is this technique called?
items.why: In the **pull-apart method**, material is pressed between two slides that are then separated in opposite directions, spreading thick or sticky specimens into two even smears. Both smears are fixed immediately while still wet.

whyNot.0: A touch preparation is made by pressing a cut tissue surface onto a slide, not by spreading fluid between slides.
whyNot.1: A cell block is a paraffin-embedded clot or pellet of sediment, not a smear.
whyNot.3: Cytocentrifugation concentrates cells from thin, low-cellularity fluids onto a small area.

items.ref: Koss' Diagnostic Cytology and Its Histopathologic Bases, 5th ed. (Laboratory techniques: respiratory specimens)

items.stem: A 'sputum' specimen for lung cancer cytology contains only superficial squamous cells and oral bacteria. Which cell, if present, would show that material from the lower respiratory tract was obtained?
items.why: **Alveolar macrophages** (dust cells), often containing carbon pigment, come from the deep airways. Their absence means the sample is mostly saliva and is not adequate for evaluation.

whyNot.0: Superficial squamous cells come from the mouth and indicate saliva, not deep sputum.
whyNot.2: Neutrophils can come from the mouth or upper airway and do not prove a deep sample.
whyNot.3: Candida commonly comes from the mouth and does not show that material came from the lungs.

items.ref: Koss' Diagnostic Cytology and Its Histopathologic Bases, 5th ed. (Respiratory tract: specimen adequacy)

items.stem: A vaginal smear shows squamous cells whose borders are blurred by a carpet of tiny coccobacilli, with few lactobacilli in the background. Under The Bethesda System, this is reported as:
options: Cellular changes consistent with herpes simplex virus
Shift in flora suggestive of bacterial vaginosis
items.why: Squamous cells covered by coccobacilli are clue cells, and loss of lactobacilli completes the picture. Bethesda reports this as a **shift in flora suggestive of bacterial vaginosis**, often associated with Gardnerella.

whyNot.0: Candida shows budding yeasts and pseudohyphae, not a coating of coccobacilli.
whyNot.1: Trichomonas appears as pear-shaped, gray-green organisms with eccentric nuclei, not as coccobacilli covering cells.
whyNot.2: Herpes causes multinucleation, nuclear molding and ground-glass chromatin in the infected cells.

items.ref: The Bethesda System for Reporting Cervical Cytology, 3rd ed. (2014 terminology) (Organisms); Koss' Diagnostic Cytology and Its Histopathologic Bases, 5th ed. (Inflammatory processes)

items.stem: In a Pap-stained sputum smear, some malignant squamous cells have dense, bright orange cytoplasm caused by keratinization. Which dye in the Papanicolaou stain gives this color?
items.why: **Orange G (OG-6)** is a small acidic dye that stains keratin bright orange, so keratinized benign or malignant squamous cells appear orange. This orangeophilia is an important clue to keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma.

whyNot.0: Eosin Y in the EA counterstain gives mature superficial cells, nucleoli and cilia a pink color, not keratin orange.
whyNot.2: Light green SF stains metabolically active, less mature cells blue-green.
whyNot.3: Bismarck brown contributes little to the final colors and does not produce bright orange keratin.

items.ref: Koss' Diagnostic Cytology and Its Histopathologic Bases, 5th ed. (Laboratory techniques: Papanicolaou stain); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Cytology)

items.stem: A cytology laboratory screens cervical smears under ultraviolet light after staining with the fluorochrome acridine orange. Cells rich in cytoplasmic RNA, such as actively dividing or malignant cells, stand out because their RNA fluoresces:
items.why: Acridine orange binds nucleic acids and fluoresces differently depending on how it binds: DNA in the nuclei gives yellow-green fluorescence, while **RNA gives orange-red fluorescence**. RNA-rich cells therefore glow orange-red and are easy to pick out for closer review.

whyNot.1: Apple-green is the birefringence of Congo red–stained amyloid under polarized light, not acridine orange fluorescence.
whyNot.2: Acridine orange does not give blue fluorescence; blue nuclear fluorescence is typical of DNA dyes such as DAPI or Hoechst.
whyNot.3: Yellow-green is the fluorescence of DNA in the nuclei, not of cytoplasmic RNA.

items.ref: Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Cytologic techniques: fluorescent staining); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Fluorescence microscopy)

items.stem: At autopsy, a mass in a pulmonary artery branch is firmly attached to the vessel wall. Microscopy shows alternating pale layers of platelets and fibrin and darker layers of red cells. These alternating layers are known as:
options: Lines of Zahn, marking an antemortem thrombus
Currant-jelly clot, marking a postmortem clot
Chicken-fat clot, marking a postmortem clot
items.why: Thrombi that form in flowing blood during life build up in layers, producing **lines of Zahn**, and they are attached to the vessel wall. Postmortem clots lack these laminations and are rubbery, unattached, with a dark red currant-jelly part and a yellow chicken-fat upper layer.

whyNot.0: Livor mortis is the purplish discoloration of dependent skin after death, not a finding inside a vessel.
