whyNot.2: Currant-jelly clot is the dark red, unlaminated part of a postmortem clot formed by settled red cells.
whyNot.3: Chicken-fat clot is the yellow, plasma-rich upper part of a postmortem clot and has no alternating layers.

items.ref: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed. (Hemodynamic disorders: thrombosis)

items.stem: In one classic autopsy technique, each organ is removed from the body separately, one at a time, and then examined and dissected individually. This method is credited to:
items.why: In the **Virchow technique**, organs are taken out one by one and dissected individually. It is simple and fast but can make it harder to show how disease in neighboring organs is related.

whyNot.1: Ghon's technique removes organs in functional blocks, such as the thoracic, abdominal and urogenital blocks (en bloc).
whyNot.2: Rokitansky's technique examines organs largely by dissection in situ, within the body.
whyNot.3: Letulle's technique removes thoracic, cervical, abdominal and pelvic organs together as one mass (en masse).

items.ref: Ludwig, Handbook of Autopsy Practice; Bruce-Gregorios, Histopathologic Techniques (Autopsy)

items.stem: In each immunohistochemistry run, a serial section of the patient tissue receives all reagents except that the primary antibody is replaced by antibody diluent or non-immune serum of the same species. What does this slide serve as?
options: A positive control showing the antibody works
An internal control within the patient tissue
A negative reagent control showing background staining
A check on the hematoxylin counterstain
items.why: Leaving out the specific primary antibody shows any staining caused by the detection system, endogenous enzymes or non-specific binding. It is a **negative reagent control**, and any brown staining on it means patient staining cannot be assumed to be specific.

whyNot.0: A positive control is a known antigen-containing tissue stained with the primary antibody to prove the run works.
whyNot.1: An internal control is a normal structure within the same section that is expected to stain, or not stain, with the antibody.
whyNot.3: The counterstain is checked on every slide; it is not the purpose of omitting the primary antibody.

items.ref: Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Immunohistochemistry: controls); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Immunohistochemical techniques)

items.stem: An estrogen receptor stain on a breast core biopsy shows the carcinoma completely negative. The benign ducts in the same section, which normally show some positive nuclei, are also negative, while the external positive control slide stained well. What is the best interpretation?
options: The external control has failed and the run is invalid
The negative result is unreliable; repeat on another block
The tumor is ER-negative and can be reported as such
The benign ducts prove the tumor is a triple-negative type
items.why: Normal breast epithelium acts as an internal positive control for ER. When **both tumor and normal ducts are negative while the external control works, the problem probably lies with that specimen (such as delayed or poor fixation), so the negative result should not be reported as reliable** and testing should be repeated on another block or specimen.

whyNot.0: The external control stained well, so the reagents and run are not at fault.
whyNot.2: Reporting ER-negative ignores the failed internal control and could deny the patient hormone therapy.
whyNot.3: The benign ducts are expected to contain some ER-positive nuclei; their negativity points to a technical problem, not a tumor type.

items.ref: ASCO/CAP Guideline for ER and PgR Testing in Breast Cancer (2020); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Immunohistochemistry)

items.stem: At the start of the day, a shiny metallic film is seen on the surface of the Harris hematoxylin in the staining line. What should be done before staining?
options: Dilute the hematoxylin with an equal volume of water
Filter the hematoxylin to remove the oxidized film
Heat the hematoxylin until the film dissolves
Add more acid alcohol to the hematoxylin
items.why: The metallic sheen is oxidized dye that forms on the surface and would otherwise be deposited on the slides as dark precipitate. The **hematoxylin should be filtered before use** (or the film skimmed off), as part of daily staining quality control.

whyNot.0: Diluting the stain weakens nuclear staining and does not remove the precipitate.
whyNot.2: Heating does not remove the oxidized film and may over-oxidize the hematoxylin.
whyNot.3: Acid alcohol is the differentiator and should never be added to the stain itself.

items.ref: Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Nuclear and cytoplasmic staining); Bancroft's Theory and Practice of Histological Techniques, 8th ed. (Hematoxylin and eosin)

items.stem: Which of the following activities is a form of external quality assessment for a histopathology laboratory?
options: Recording the water bath temperature every morning
Taking part in an interlaboratory proficiency testing scheme
Performing scheduled maintenance on the tissue processor
Staining a known control section in each special stain run
items.why: In **proficiency testing (external quality assessment)**, an outside provider sends slides or cases that many laboratories stain or interpret, and each laboratory's results are compared with the others. The other options are internal quality control activities done within the laboratory.

whyNot.0: Temperature logs are internal monitoring of equipment, not external assessment.
whyNot.2: Preventive maintenance is an internal quality practice for equipment.
whyNot.3: Running a control slide with each batch is internal quality control.

items.ref: CLSI QMS01 (Quality management system model); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Laboratory quality)

items.stem: A specimen container arrives labeled with the patient's name only, while the requisition lists the name, hospital number and date of birth. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Process it, since the name matches the requisition
Discard it and ask for a repeat biopsy
Write the hospital number on the container from the requisition
Hold the specimen and have the sender correct the labeling
items.why: Specimen identification requires at least two patient identifiers on both the container and the requisition. A biopsy often cannot be repeated, so the laboratory should **hold the specimen (in fixative) and have the submitting team correct the labeling following the documented procedure** before processing.

whyNot.0: A name alone is not enough to rule out a mix-up between patients with similar or identical names.
whyNot.1: Discarding an irreplaceable tissue specimen is never the first step when labeling can be corrected properly.
whyNot.2: Laboratory staff should not add identifiers themselves; that is how mislabeling errors are hidden rather than fixed.

items.ref: CAP Anatomic Pathology Checklist (specimen identification); Carson & Cappellano, Histotechnology: A Self-Instructional Text, 5th ed. (Laboratory quality)

items.stem: An examinee's board ratings are: Clinical Chemistry 70, Microbiology & Parasitology 70, Hematology 72, Blood Banking & Serology 72, Clinical Microscopy 90, and Histopathologic Techniques/Cytotechnology/MT Laws & Ethics 86. Using the subject weights in Section 17 of RA 5527 (as amended by PD 498), what is the general average, and did the examinee pass under Section 19?
items.why: Clinical Chemistry, Microbiology & Parasitology, Hematology and Blood Banking & Serology each carry 20%, while Clinical Microscopy and the histopathology/laws subject carry 10% each. Weighted average = 0.20(70 + 70 + 72 + 72) + 0.10(90 + 86) = 56.8 + 17.6 = **74.4%, which is below the 75% general average required to pass**. Having no rating below 50% does not make up for this, and the four 20% subjects, all rated below 75%, also mean the examinee failed 80% of the subjects by weight, beyond what the Section 19 proviso allows.

whyNot.1: 76.7% is the simple (unweighted) mean of the six ratings. Section 19 uses the Section 17 weights, so high scores in the two 10% subjects count for less.
whyNot.2: Having no subject below 50% is only one of the passing conditions. The weighted general average must also reach 75%.
whyNot.3: 76.7% comes from the unweighted mean, which is the wrong way to compute the general average, so the figure itself is wrong.

items.ref: RA 5527 Secs. 17 and 19 (Sec. 17 as amended by PD 498, 1974)

worked.problem: Ratings: Clinical Chemistry 78, Microbiology & Parasitology 80, Hematology 76, Blood Banking & Serology 74, Clinical Microscopy 65, Histopathologic Techniques/Laws & Ethics 70. What is the weighted general average, and does the examinee pass?
steps: Subjects below 75% (Blood Banking & Serology 20%, Clinical Microscopy 10%, Histopathologic Techniques/Laws 10%) total 40% of the weights, under the 60% limit in the Section 19 proviso.
worked.result: 75.1%: passes (average at least 75%, no subject below 50%, failed subjects under 60% by weight)

items.stem: To keep up with molecular diagnostics, the Board of Medical Technology wants to add a new subject area to the licensure examination. Under Section 17 of RA 5527 as amended by PD 498, what is required before the change can apply to an examination?
options: An amendment of RA 5527 by Congress, since the law fixes the exam subjects
A majority vote of the members of the accredited professional organization
Prior PRC approval, and publication of the change at least three months before the exam
Publication of the change at least 30 days before the exam, with no further approval
items.why: PD 498 lets the Board change, add to, or remove subjects from the examination as the science of medical technology advances. It may do so only with **prior approval of the Professional Regulation Commission and publication of the change at least three months before the examination**. This gives examinees fair notice of what will be tested.

whyNot.0: No new act of Congress is needed. Section 17 itself already gives the Board authority to revise the subjects.
whyNot.1: The professional organization has no approving role over examination subjects under Section 17.
whyNot.3: Thirty days is the notice period for announcing the examination itself (Section 15). Subject changes need PRC approval and three months' publication.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 17, as amended by PD 498 (1974)

items.stem: Under Section 15 of RA 5527, how must the Secretary of the Board give notice of an upcoming medical technology licensure examination?
options: Publication in one national newspaper, 10 or more days before the exam
Publication in at least three national newspapers, 30 or more days before the exam
Posting in every school of medical technology, 7 or more days before the exam
Registered mail to each applicant, 60 or more days before the exam
items.why: Section 15 requires the Secretary of the Board to publish **written notice in at least three newspapers of national circulation at least thirty days before the examination**. This gives applicants nationwide enough time to prepare and file.

whyNot.0: One newspaper and 10 days fall short of both the number of newspapers and the lead time the law requires.
whyNot.2: The law requires publication in national newspapers, not posting in schools, and a 30-day lead time.
whyNot.3: Section 15 does not require individual mailed notices. It requires newspaper publication at least 30 days ahead.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 15

items.stem: A newly successful board examinee wants to start working as a medical technologist as soon as the results are released. Under Section 20 of RA 5527, what must she do before entering practice?
options: Complete a one-year probationary period under a pathologist
Join the accredited professional organization of medical technologists
Pass a separate practical examination given by the employing hospital
Take a professional oath before the Board or a person authorized to administer oaths
items.why: Section 20 requires every successful examinee to **take a professional oath before the Board or before any person authorized to administer oaths** before entering the practice of medical technology. The oath is a legal precondition to practice, alongside registration under Section 21.

whyNot.0: RA 5527 has no post-examination probationary period. Supervision by a pathologist is part of practice, not a step before it.
whyNot.1: Membership in a professional organization is not what Section 20 requires before practice.
whyNot.2: Employers may test applicants, but the law does not require a second examination before a successful examinee can practice.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 20

items.stem: A hospital HR officer wants to confirm that a job applicant is a registered medical technologist. Under Section 28 of RA 5527, which record is prepared for this kind of public checking?
options: The yearly roster of medical technologists kept by the Board
The applicant's official transcript of records from her school
The membership list of the national professional organization
The credentials file kept by the applicant's previous employer
items.why: Section 28 requires the Secretary of the Board to prepare a roster every year listing each registered medical technologist's name, address, citizenship, date of registration and other pertinent data. **The roster is open to public inspection**, and copies go to government offices on request.

whyNot.1: A transcript shows that she graduated, not that she passed the board and is registered.
whyNot.2: Membership in a professional organization is separate from registration with the Board.
whyNot.3: A previous employer's file is not an official registration record and may be outdated or incomplete.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 28

items.stem: A foreign medical technologist applies to take the Philippine medical technology licensure examination. Under Section 27 of RA 5527, on what condition may she be admitted?
options: She has worked for at least five years in a Philippine hospital laboratory
She is married to a Filipino citizen and has lived in the Philippines for five years
Her country allows Filipino medical technologists to practice there on equal terms
She passes an English proficiency test administered by the Professional Regulation Commission
items.why: Section 27 sets a rule of **reciprocity**. No foreigner may be admitted to the examination, registered, or given practice rights unless his or her country allows Filipino medical technologists to practice there on the same basis as its own citizens.

whyNot.0: Prior local work experience is not the test under Section 27, and practicing without registration would itself be unlawful.
whyNot.1: Marriage to a Filipino does not satisfy the reciprocity requirement in Section 27.
whyNot.3: RA 5527 has no language-test condition for foreigners. The deciding factor is reciprocity.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 27

items.stem: Twelve months have passed since a medical technologist began serving a one-year Board suspension. Under Section 26 of RA 5527, where does that leave her registration?
options: She must retake and pass the board examination before practicing again
The suspension ends automatically, and the certificate is reissued to her on request
She must wait another year and then petition the Board for reinstatement
The suspension becomes permanent unless the PRC Chairperson lifts it
items.why: Under Section 26, **a suspension terminates automatically when the suspension period expires**, and the certificate is reissued to the technologist on request. The Board may still act on any violation committed during the suspension. A revoked certificate is different: it is reissued only if the Board finds the application meritorious.

whyNot.0: Re-examination is not required after a suspension ends. She remains registered.
whyNot.2: No extra waiting period or petition is needed, because the suspension ends on its own.
whyNot.3: A suspension cannot become permanent by default. The law limits it to a fixed period of at most two years.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 26 (see also Sec. 24)

items.stem: A hospital laboratory assigns a duly registered medical laboratory technician (MLT) to do tissue processing, embedding and section cutting. Under Section 2 of RA 5527 as amended by PD 498, is this allowed?
options: No; histopathologic techniques may be done only by registered medical technologists
No; only a pathologist may perform any step of tissue processing
Yes, but only if the MLT has passed a separate PRC histotechnology examination
Yes; the law expressly does not bar a registered MLT from histopathologic techniques
items.why: PD 498 lists histopathologic techniques and cytotechnology among the procedures that make up the practice of medical technology. It then adds a proviso that **nothing in that paragraph prevents a duly registered medical laboratory technician from performing histopathologic techniques**. The MLT still works as an assistant to the medical technologist, as Section 2(d) defines the role.

whyNot.0: This ignores the PD 498 proviso that specifically keeps histopathologic techniques open to registered MLTs.
whyNot.1: Pathologists interpret tissue and supervise, but the law does not reserve the technical steps of tissue processing to them.
whyNot.2: RA 5527 has no separate histotechnology examination. The MLT's registration is enough under the proviso.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 2(a)(4) and 2(d), as amended by PD 498 (1974)

items.stem: The Board's ruling against a medical technologist is now final and executory. Under Section 24 of RA 5527, by when must she hand in her certificate, and what is the consequence of an unjustified failure to do so?
options: Within 30 days after the decision becomes final; otherwise, perpetual disqualification from practice
Within 30 days after the decision becomes final; otherwise, the suspension period is doubled
Within 90 days after the hearing ends; otherwise, perpetual disqualification from practice
Within 90 days after the hearing ends; otherwise, a fine of ₱2,000–₱5,000
items.why: Section 24 requires a suspended or revoked medical technologist to surrender the certificate within 30 days after the decision becomes final. Failure to do so without satisfactory reason means **perpetual disqualification from the practice of medical technology in the Philippines**. The suspension period runs only from the date of surrender, so keeping the certificate gains nothing.

whyNot.1: The 30-day period is correct, but the law does not double the suspension. The consequence is perpetual disqualification.
whyNot.2: The penalty is right, but the period is counted as 30 days from the date the decision becomes final, not 90 days from the hearing.
whyNot.3: Both the period and the consequence are wrong. The ₱2,000–₱5,000 fine is the criminal penalty under Section 29, not the sanction for failing to surrender.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 24

items.stem: The owner of a private clinical laboratory hires a BS Medical Technology graduate who has not yet passed the board examination and lets him perform and release laboratory tests. Under Section 29 of RA 5527 as amended by PD 498, who may be penalized?
options: Only the graduate, since the owner did not personally perform the tests
Only the owner, since a graduate cannot be liable before registration
Both the unregistered graduate and the owner who allowed him to practice
Neither, because graduates awaiting the board exam are exempt
items.why: Section 29 penalizes anyone who practices medical technology without a certificate of registration. PD 498 amended item (j) to also penalize anyone who **allows an unregistered person in his employ to engage in the practice of medical technology**. The penalty is a fine of ₱2,000–₱5,000, imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years, or both.

whyNot.0: PD 498 specifically made the employer who allows unregistered practice liable as well.
whyNot.1: Practicing without registration is itself a violation, so the graduate is also liable.
whyNot.3: Section 14 exempts only specific groups, such as registered physicians and certain visiting foreign professionals. Graduates awaiting the board exam are not among them.

items.ref: RA 5527 Sec. 29, as amended by PD 498 (1974); Sec. 14

items.stem: The Philippine HIV and AIDS Policy Act (RA 11166) generally prohibits compulsory HIV testing. In which situation does the law allow HIV testing without the person's consent?
options: As a pre-employment requirement of a private company
Screening of blood or organs offered for donation
As a requirement for admission to a college or university
Routine screening of all patients on hospital admission
items.why: Section 30 of RA 11166 bans compulsory HIV testing except in a few cases: persons charged with certain crimes involving physical injuries or sexual offenses, determining HIV status to resolve certain issues under the Family Code, and **screening of donated blood, organs and tissues under RA 7170 and RA 7719**. Every other HIV test needs informed consent.

whyNot.0: Requiring an HIV test as a condition of employment is compulsory testing, which the law prohibits.
whyNot.2: School admission is not an exception. Requiring HIV testing for enrollment is prohibited compulsory testing.
whyNot.3: Hospital admission is not an exception. Patients must still give informed consent to an HIV test.

items.ref: RA 11166 Sec. 30 (see also Sec. 29)

items.stem: Section 36 of RA 9165 separates groups that must be tested from groups tested by random selection. Which of these groups falls under random selection?
options: People applying for a new or renewed driver's license
People seeking a permit to own or carry a gun
Uniformed personnel of the PNP and the AFP
items.why: Section 36 provides **random drug testing for students of secondary and tertiary schools**, done according to the school's student handbook, with notice to parents and at government expense. Officers and employees of public and private offices are also tested at random. License applicants and members of the military, police and other law enforcement agencies undergo mandatory testing.

whyNot.0: Driver's license applicants undergo mandatory testing and must present a drug test certificate before a license is issued or renewed.
whyNot.1: Firearms license applicants undergo mandatory testing before a license or permit is issued.
whyNot.2: Members of the military, police and other law enforcement agencies undergo mandatory annual drug testing.

items.ref: RA 9165 Sec. 36

items.stem: A job applicant's urine drug screen at an accredited screening laboratory is positive for methamphetamine. Under Section 36 of RA 9165, what must happen before the result is treated as a positive drug test?
options: A confirmatory test must confirm the positive screening result
The same screening test must be repeated twice more on the specimen
The applicant must sign a written admission of drug use
A physician must examine the applicant for signs of intoxication
items.why: Section 36 states that drug testing uses two methods: a screening test, and **a confirmatory test that confirms a positive screening test**. The confirmatory test is done by a government forensic laboratory or a DOH-accredited confirmatory laboratory, typically using GC-MS. A screen alone is not a final positive.

whyNot.1: Repeating the same screening method does not confirm the result. A different, more specific confirmatory method is required.
whyNot.2: An admission is not part of the testing process the law prescribes.
whyNot.3: A clinical examination cannot replace the confirmatory laboratory test that the law requires.

items.ref: RA 9165 Sec. 36 (see also Sec. 38)

items.stem: A baby born at 30 weeks is admitted to the neonatal ICU right after delivery and is too unstable for routine procedures during her first three days. Under the Newborn Screening Act of 2004 (RA 9288), what applies to her newborn screening?
options: Screening is skipped and done only if symptoms appear later
Screening must still be done within 3 days, regardless of her condition
She may be exempted from the 3-day limit, but must be screened by 7 days of age
Screening is postponed until she is discharged from the NICU, however long that takes
items.why: Section 6 sets screening after 24 hours of life but not later than three days from complete delivery. However, **a newborn placed in intensive care to ensure survival may be exempted from the 3-day requirement but must be screened by 7 days of age**. Parents and the attending practitioner share responsibility for getting it done.

whyNot.0: Screening is meant to find heritable conditions before symptoms appear. Skipping it defeats the purpose of the Act.
whyNot.1: The law expressly allows an exception to the 3-day limit for infants in intensive care.
whyNot.3: The exception is limited. Even an infant in intensive care must be screened by 7 days of age.

items.ref: RA 9288 Sec. 6

items.stem: A patient notices that her laboratory report shows the wrong birth date. She asks the laboratory to fix it in its information system and to let her physician, who already received the report, know about the fix. Under the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173), which right is she exercising?
options: Right to dispute inaccuracy and have the data corrected
Right to be informed before her data are processed
Right to be indemnified for damages
items.why: Section 16(d) gives the data subject the **right to dispute an inaccuracy or error in her personal information and have the controller correct it**. On her reasonable request, third parties who already received the data, such as her physician, must be told of the inaccuracy and the correction.

whyNot.0: Data portability (Section 18) means getting a copy of her electronically processed data in a structured format, not correcting it.
whyNot.2: The right to be informed concerns being told the purpose and scope of processing before or when data are collected.
whyNot.3: Indemnification is compensation for damages from inaccurate or unauthorized use of data, which she is not seeking here.

items.ref: RA 10173 Sec. 16(d) (see also Sec. 18)

items.stem: Under Section 12 of the National Blood Services Act of 1994 (RA 7719), a blood bank head, and the trained staff under his direct supervision, who dispense or transfuse blood proven contaminated with a transfusion-transmissible disease, or who fail to dispose of it within a set period, face 10 years' imprisonment. What is that disposal period?
items.why: Section 12 penalizes with 10 years' imprisonment the blood bank head and trained staff under his direct supervision who are responsible for dispensing, transfusing, or **failing to dispose of within 48 hours** blood proven contaminated with transfusion-transmissible disease. This is without prejudice to liability under the Revised Penal Code.

whyNot.0: Twenty-four hours is shorter than the period stated in Section 12.
whyNot.2: Seventy-two hours is longer than the 48 hours the law allows.
whyNot.3: Seven days is far beyond the 48-hour limit set by Section 12.

items.ref: RA 7719 Sec. 12

items.stem: A 17-year-old student of sound mind wants to sign a donor card leaving her kidneys for transplantation after her death. Under Section 3 of the Organ Donation Act of 1991 (RA 7170), can she make this legacy on her own?
options: Yes; any person of sound mind may make a legacy, whatever her age
Yes; the minimum age is 15 years for a person of sound mind
No; the person must be at least 21 years old and of sound mind
No; the person must be at least 18 years old and of sound mind
items.why: Section 3 allows **any individual at least 18 years of age and of sound mind** to give all or part of his or her body by legacy, effective after death. At 17 she does not yet qualify, but she may execute the legacy once she turns 18, for example by a signed donor card (Section 8).

whyNot.0: The law sets a minimum age, so being of sound mind alone is not enough.
whyNot.1: Fifteen is not the age set by RA 7170. Ages 15 to 17 appear in RA 11166 for consenting to HIV testing, not here.
whyNot.2: Twenty-one is too high. It is the minimum age for a medical technologist's certificate of registration under RA 5527.

items.ref: RA 7170 Sec. 3 (amended by RA 7885 only in Secs. 9–10)

items.stem: A medical technologist attends a two-day hospital-sponsored training course on a new analyzer. The course was never accredited by the CPD Council, but she later applies to have it credited. Under RA 10912, this kind of activity is classified as:
items.why: Section 3(w) of RA 10912 defines **self-directed learning** as activities such as online training, local or international seminars or non-degree courses, and institution- or company-sponsored training that did not undergo CPD accreditation, but for which CPD units may be applied for and awarded.

whyNot.0: Formal learning refers to curricular programs in recognized education and training institutions that lead to diplomas and qualifications.
whyNot.1: Informal learning is learning that happens in daily life and is later assessed, recognized and validated. It is not a structured course.
whyNot.2: An accredited CPD program is a set of learning activities already accredited by the CPD Council, which this course was not.

items.ref: RA 10912 Sec. 3(w); compare Sec. 3(i), (k), (l)

items.stem: When renewing her professional ID, a medical technologist submits a fake certificate of attendance to claim CPD units for a seminar she never attended. Under Section 16 of RA 10912, what may she face?
options: Prosecution under the Revised Penal Code and other laws, plus suspension or revocation of her registration
Only a written reprimand from the CPD Council, since CPD matters are purely administrative
Forfeiture of the falsely claimed units, with no other sanction
A fixed fine of ₱5,000 payable to the CPD provider named on the certificate
items.why: Section 16 makes fraudulent acts related to CPD punishable under the Revised Penal Code, the New Civil Code and other applicable laws. On top of these, a guilty professional faces **suspension or revocation of the PRC certificate of registration** and/or certificate of specialization.

whyNot.1: CPD fraud is not purely administrative. The Act refers it to penal and civil laws as well.
whyNot.2: Losing the false units is not the only consequence. Registration itself may be suspended or revoked.
whyNot.3: RA 10912 sets no fixed fine payable to a provider. Penalties come from existing laws plus action against the registration.

items.stem: Under the PRC Modernization Act of 2000 (RA 8981), what is the term of office of the PRC Chairperson and the two Commissioners?
options: Until age 65, with no fixed term
items.why: Section 5 of RA 8981 fixes the term of the Chairperson and Commissioners at **seven years without reappointment**. A person appointed to fill a vacancy serves only the unexpired term.

whyNot.0: Three years is the term of members of the Board of Medical Technology under RA 5527, not of the Commission.
whyNot.1: Five years appears in RA 8981 only as the minimum executive or management experience required of appointees, not as the term.
whyNot.3: The Commission's members serve a fixed seven-year term, not until a retirement age.

items.ref: RA 8981 Secs. 4–5

items.stem: A patient asks why she must have her blood drawn again. The real reason is that the laboratory mislabeled her first sample. Instead of blaming a 'machine problem,' the medical technologist tells her the truth and apologizes. Which ethical principle does this most directly show?
items.why: **Veracity** is the duty to tell the truth and not to deceive patients. Honest disclosure of an error, even an embarrassing one, maintains the trust that the professional-patient relationship depends on.

whyNot.1: Justice is about fair distribution of benefits and burdens and equal treatment, not truthful disclosure.
whyNot.2: Fidelity is about keeping promises and loyalty to commitments. Here the key act is not deceiving the patient.
whyNot.3: Autonomy is respect for the patient's own informed decisions. The central act here is honesty, though honesty does support autonomy.

items.ref: Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics (Veracity)

items.stem: A mentally competent adult has asked to be told her biopsy result. Her physician decides not to tell her that it shows cancer, because he believes the news would harm her. Overriding a competent person's known wishes for that person's own supposed good is called:
items.why: Paternalism is the intentional overriding of a person's known preferences or actions, justified by the aim of benefiting that person or preventing harm to them. It sets **beneficence in conflict with respect for autonomy**. For a competent adult who has asked to know, withholding the result is hard to justify.

whyNot.0: Respect for autonomy would mean honoring her request to know the result, which is the opposite of what the physician did.
whyNot.1: Veracity, the duty to tell the truth, is what the physician is setting aside, not what he is applying.
whyNot.2: Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of resources among people, not one patient's access to her own results.

items.ref: Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics (Beneficence: paternalism)

items.stem: A terminally ill patient in severe pain receives high-dose opioids intended only to relieve the pain, although the physician foresees that the drug may depress breathing and hasten death. Which principle is classically used to justify this?
items.why: The **rule of double effect** permits an act with a good and a bad effect if the act itself is not wrong, only the good effect is intended, the bad effect is not the means to the good effect, and there is a proportionate reason. Pain relief is intended. Respiratory depression is foreseen but not intended, and it is not how the pain is relieved.

whyNot.0: The principle of totality justifies sacrificing a part of the body, as in amputation, for the good of the whole person. It does not deal with foreseen side effects.
whyNot.2: Distributive justice is about fair allocation of resources among patients, not about weighing the effects of one treatment.
whyNot.3: Patient consent matters, but autonomy alone does not explain why a foreseen harmful side effect can be acceptable.

items.ref: Beauchamp & Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics (Nonmaleficence: rule of double effect)

items.stem: A medical technologist who works full time in a hospital laboratory is offered a weekend job at a private clinic. Under the Code of Ethics for medical technologists, when may she accept a second employer?
options: Never; a medical technologist may serve only one employer at a time
Only after the PRC issues a special permit for dual employment
Only when there is no conflict of interest between the two jobs
Anytime, since work outside regular hours is not covered by the code
items.why: The medical technologists' code of ethics allows a medical technologist to **accept employment from more than one employer only when there is no conflict of interest**. For example, a second job should not compete with, or compromise her duties and confidentiality obligations to, the first employer.

whyNot.0: The code does not forbid multiple employment outright. It conditions it on the absence of conflict of interest.
whyNot.1: No special PRC permit for dual employment exists. A valid registration already allows her to practice.
whyNot.3: The code's obligations apply to all professional work, not only to work done during regular hours.

items.ref: PAMET Code of Ethics for Medical Technologists (1997); PRBMT Resolution No. 72, s. 2022 (Code of Ethics of the Medical Technology Profession)

items.stem: A medical technologist notices that a coworker keeps releasing patient glucose results on days when the controls failed and were never rerun. According to the medical technologists' Code of Ethics, what should she do?
options: Report the infraction to the proper authority, such as the laboratory head or ethics committee
Post an anonymous warning about the laboratory on social media
Say nothing, since criticizing a colleague goes against professional courtesy
Quietly rerun and replace the coworker's results without telling anyone
items.why: The code commits medical technologists to **report infractions of professional conduct to the authorities responsible**, while keeping criticism of others within constructive limits. Releasing results after failed QC endangers patients, so silence is not an option.

whyNot.1: Public posting bypasses proper channels, can breach confidentiality, and goes beyond constructive criticism.
whyNot.2: Professional courtesy does not override the duty to report conduct that puts patients at risk.
whyNot.3: Secretly changing results hides the problem, leaves the cause uncorrected, and is itself improper documentation.

items.ref: PAMET Code of Ethics for Medical Technologists (1997); PRBMT Resolution No. 72, s. 2022 (Code of Ethics of the Medical Technology Profession), Art. III Sec. 4

items.stem: A laboratory is pricing a new test. Fixed costs for it (instrument lease and allocated salaries) are ₱180,000 per month. Reagents and supplies cost ₱150 per test, and the laboratory will charge ₱450 per test. How many tests per month must it perform to break even?
items.why: Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per test) = 180,000 ÷ (450 − 150) = **600 tests per month**. Each test contributes ₱300 toward the fixed costs, and 600 × ₱300 covers the ₱180,000.

whyNot.0: 400 tests (180,000 ÷ 450) ignores the ₱150 variable cost that each test uses up.
whyNot.2: 1,200 tests (180,000 ÷ 150) divides by the variable cost instead of by the contribution margin.
whyNot.3: 300 tests (180,000 ÷ 600) wrongly adds the variable cost to the price instead of subtracting it.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Financial management: break-even analysis)

worked.problem: Fixed costs are ₱120,000 per month, the price is ₱350 per test, and the variable cost is ₱110 per test. What is the break-even volume?

items.stem: A laboratory uses an average of 25 blood culture bottles per day. The supplier's lead time is 6 days, and the laboratory keeps a safety stock of 50 bottles. At what stock level should a new order be placed?
items.why: Reorder point = (average daily usage × lead time) + safety stock = (25 × 6) + 50 = **200 bottles**. Ordering at this level covers use during the 6-day wait and still leaves the safety stock as a buffer against delays or surges.

whyNot.0: 75 bottles is one day's use plus the safety stock, which runs out long before a 6-day delivery arrives.
whyNot.1: 150 bottles covers use during the lead time but leaves out the 50-bottle safety stock.
whyNot.3: 300 bottles counts the lead-time demand twice (25 × 6 × 2), which ties up money and storage space.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Inventory management); CLSI QMS01

worked.problem: A section uses 12 reagent cartridges per day. Lead time is 10 days and safety stock is 30 cartridges. What is the reorder point?

items.stem: A technologist receives new reagent kits that expire in 10 months. The shelf still holds kits of the same reagent that expire in 3 months. How should the stock be used?
options: Use the new kits first, because fresher reagents are more reliable
Open one kit from each lot at the same time for comparison
Discard the older kits now that the new shipment has arrived
Use the 3-month kits first, then the new kits, by expiry date
items.why: Stock is rotated so that **the lots expiring soonest are used first** (first-expired, first-out, closely related to FIFO). The new kits are placed behind the older ones. This prevents reagents from expiring unused on the shelf.

whyNot.0: Using new kits first lets the older, still-valid kits expire and be wasted.
whyNot.1: Opening several lots at once shortens their open-vial stability and does not solve the rotation problem.
whyNot.2: The older kits are still within their expiry date. Discarding them wastes money.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Inventory management); CLSI QMS01 (Purchasing and inventory)

items.stem: A laboratory tallied 600 rejected specimens over three months by reason: hemolysis, clotting, mislabeling, insufficient volume and wrong tube. The manager wants to see which few reasons account for most rejections so that improvement efforts can be focused. Which quality tool is designed for this?
items.why: A **Pareto chart** shows categories as bars in descending order of frequency, with a cumulative-percentage line, so the 'vital few' causes behind most of the problem stand out (the 80/20 rule).

whyNot.1: A Levey-Jennings chart plots control results over time to monitor analytical QC, not to rank problem categories.
whyNot.2: A Gantt chart schedules project tasks over time.
whyNot.3: A fishbone diagram brainstorms the possible causes of one problem but does not rank causes by how often they occur.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Quality management tools); CLSI QMS01

items.stem: A hospital laboratory wants international accreditation that covers both its quality management system and the technical competence of its clinical testing. Which standard is written specifically for this?
items.why: **ISO 15189** sets requirements for quality and competence in medical laboratories. It combines quality management system requirements with technical requirements specific to clinical testing, across the pre-examination, examination and post-examination phases.

whyNot.0: ISO 9001 is a general quality management standard for any organization. It certifies the system but not technical testing competence.
whyNot.1: ISO/IEC 17025 covers testing and calibration laboratories in general. ISO 15189 is the version tailored to medical laboratories.
whyNot.3: ISO 14001 deals with environmental management systems.

items.ref: ISO 15189:2022, Medical laboratories — Requirements for quality and competence; Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Quality management)

items.stem: After a salary increase and a renovated break room, the medical technologists in a laboratory say they are no longer dissatisfied, yet they feel no more driven to excel than before. In Herzberg's two-factor theory, salary and working conditions are:
items.why: In Herzberg's theory, hygiene factors such as pay, working conditions, policies, supervision and coworker relations **prevent dissatisfaction when adequate but do not by themselves motivate**. Motivators such as achievement, recognition, responsibility and growth are what raise motivation.

whyNot.0: Motivators are intrinsic to the work, such as achievement and recognition, not pay or surroundings.
whyNot.2: Self-actualization is the top level of Maslow's hierarchy, not a Herzberg category.
whyNot.3: Theory Y is McGregor's view of workers as self-motivated. It does not classify job factors.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Human resource management: motivation theories)

items.stem: During annual appraisals, a supervisor gives one medical technologist top marks in every category, including punctuality and documentation, mainly because she is outstanding at troubleshooting analyzers. This rating error is called:
items.why: The **halo effect** occurs when one strong positive trait colors the rater's judgment of all other, unrelated performance areas. Rating each criterion separately against written standards and documented examples helps prevent it.

whyNot.0: Central tendency error means rating everyone near the middle of the scale, avoiding high and low scores.
whyNot.1: Recency effect means letting the most recent events dominate the appraisal of the whole rating period.
whyNot.3: Contrast effect means rating an employee against the coworker evaluated just before, instead of against the standards.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Human resource management: performance appraisal)

items.stem: A laboratory Six Sigma team working on long emergency-room turnaround times has already defined the problem and collected baseline turnaround data. The team now uses a fishbone diagram and breaks down the data by shift to find the root causes of the delays. Which DMAIC phase is this?
items.why: DMAIC stands for Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve and Control. **Finding root causes from the baseline data is the Analyze phase**. Solutions are then piloted in Improve and sustained in Control.

whyNot.0: Define (stating the problem, scope and goals) was already done.
whyNot.1: Measure (collecting baseline data on the current process) was also completed before the root-cause work.
whyNot.3: Improve comes after the root causes are known, when solutions are designed and tested.

items.ref: Garcia LS (ed.), Clinical Laboratory Management, ASM Press (Quality management: Six Sigma)

items.stem: A researcher surveying medical technologists' biosafety practices wants hospital-based, free-standing and government laboratories represented in the same proportions as in the whole population. She divides the sampling frame into these three groups and then randomly selects technologists from each group. Which sampling method is this?
items.why: In **stratified random sampling**, the population is divided into subgroups (strata) that share a characteristic, and a random sample is drawn from each stratum, often in proportion to its size. This ensures each subgroup is represented.

whyNot.0: Cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups (for example, entire laboratories) and studies all or most members of the chosen groups.
whyNot.2: Quota sampling also fills subgroup targets, but selection within each subgroup is not random.
whyNot.3: Systematic sampling picks every kth person from a single ordered list, without first dividing the population into strata.

items.ref: Polit & Beck, Nursing Research: Generating and Assessing Evidence (Sampling); Gordis Epidemiology

items.stem: In the usual hierarchy of evidence for questions about whether an intervention works, which source gives the strongest evidence?
options: A large, well-designed prospective cohort study
A case series of consecutive patients from one hospital
Consensus opinion of a panel of senior pathologists
A systematic review with meta-analysis of randomized trials
items.why: For questions about therapy or intervention, **systematic reviews and meta-analyses of well-conducted randomized controlled trials** sit at the top of the evidence hierarchy. They pool trials that minimize bias through randomization.

whyNot.0: Cohort studies are observational and more prone to confounding, so they rank below randomized trials and their systematic reviews.
whyNot.1: Case series have no comparison group and rank near the bottom of the hierarchy.
whyNot.2: Expert opinion without systematic appraisal of evidence is the lowest level.

items.ref: Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine, Levels of Evidence; Polit & Beck, Nursing Research (Evidence hierarchy)
